📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, which runs from December 4 to 6, NBA star Kevin Love reflects on his journey into art collecting, which has made him the proud owner of works by Antony Gormley, Rashid Johnson, Ed Ruscha and George Condo.

In an interview with Art Basel’s Miami Beach Magazine, the five-time NBA All-Star and 2016 NBA champion and his wife, Kate Bock, opened their Miami home to reporters, displaying an impressive art collection of paintings and sculptures. He reveals that he has Ed Ruscha’s The End (2021) hanging over his bed, a painting to which he feels a personal connection. “I hate to be one of those people who watches a lot of TV in bed, but we do, and The End has a connection to Ruscha and to film. It’s also very literal: It’s the end of the day, you’re in bed,” Love said. “And it’s a reminder: I’m thinking about the end of a career. Whether it’s in two months or two years, it’s there; and with that, fresh beginnings as well. I’ve always loved his work. He’s a great man, he’s empathetic and supportive. My wedding gift to my wife, Kate, was a Ruscha.” Love is also the owner of three other Ruscha artworks: Woman on Fire (2024), He Enjoys the Co. of Women (2025) and The Girl Always Did Have Good Taste (2021). Related Articles Christie's Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy As Art Week NYC Kicks Off, Galleries Have Millions of Dollars of Art to Sell--And No Shortage of Naras.

Even though Love can’t pinpoint when his enthusiasm for art collecting started, he noted that around the 2012 Olympics he learned his peers, including Carmelo Anthony and LeBron James, were interested in art. “That made the whole world feel a little less intimidating. I asked a lot of questions. ‘Where do you start?’ ‘What should I be looking at?’” Love said, noting that art adviser Jane Suitor has always encouraged him to stay “curious.”.

In a recent development, in the magazine photo shoot, four works by Johnson are displayed: Untitled Anxious Red (2020), Run (2018), Falling Man (2015), and another painting from the Anxious Drawing series. Other pieces in his home range from Antony Gormley’s sculpture SMALL LOOK V (2015), a George Condo line drawing Untitled (2017), Richard Prince’s Untitled (Palomino) (1982–86), Hank Willis Thomas’ O! thus be it ever (2021), and John Baldessari’s Aerial View/People (1988).

In a recent development, over the years, Love has built a friendship with artists Jonas Wood and Rashid Johnson. “Jonas Wood is a crazy, avid basketball fan, and my second favorite sport is tennis, so personal stories are initially where the connection resides,” noted the basketball player. “I’m very lucky to have Rashid Johnson in my life. I first connected [with the work] for emotional reasons without knowing much about him. I’m seven minutes down the road from his studio in the Hamptons.”.

According to recent reports, in the interview, Love recalls buying his wife a neon Tracey Emin heart with the words “An Insane Desire for You” written inside. He later followed up by buying her a 10-foot Dan Flavin in all his favorite colors, which they haven’t installed yet. “Turns out my wife doesn’t like neon,” Love said.

In a recent development, at Art Basel Miami Beach, Love will be joining the likes of Brooklyn Nets and Fresh York Liberty co-owner Clara Wu Tsai, soccer player Crystal Dunn, and NFL chief marketing officer Tim Ellis in the fair’s Art & Sport day, a series of panel talks between the art and sports worlds. Love and Keith Rivers, a former professional football player, will be in conversation with each other on December 3 to discuss “when athletes become collectors.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.
  • Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.
  • Construction organization Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Kilian O’Sullivan.

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction organization Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design stated the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

In a recent development, “Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”.

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” said Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”.

It has been revealed that elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he said.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”.

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley said the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The upcoming development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently announced that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s new Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”.

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) revealed the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

Latest Update: At the Broad, Six Decades of Art Question the Myth of Progress

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1489 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities.
  • Sources indicate that more than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay.
  • Rosales’s 2024 sculpture Has the myth been shattered encases that infamous yellowed newspaper in a nearly six-foot-tall aluminum frame fitted with a two-way mirror, illuminated by colorful LED lights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities. For years, she’d witnessed the chasm widen between women carrying $3,500 handbags and those wearing trash bags; from her “nice neighborhood where the helicopters don’t come,” she did little to address the disparity. Still, the unrest that followed the acquittal of four LAPD officers charged with beating Rodney King seemed to have broken through the collective apathy. Angelenos, she wrote, were suddenly talking about “things that matter”: race, guilt, poverty, urban policy, to name a few. Despite history offering little reason for optimism, Scott confessed to a sense of hope: “I’m nurturing my first illusion.” Related Articles Christie's Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy Piaget's Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch.

Sources indicate that more than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay. The headlines “Seeing Ourselves” and “Has the Myth Been Shattered?” registered the same discrepancy she sensed between what she remembered as a child growing up in East LA and how the press perpetuated myths about the city’s seeming collectivity. Rosales was 11 years old in 1992, and she has a distinct memory of her mother rushing the family home from school as smoke stained the usually sun-drenched California sky. As an adult, Rosales has amassed an archive of clippings, photographs, and other ephemera of Chicanx youth culture—much of it crowdsourced through social media—that serves as both a bulwark against that dissonance and a counter to historical erasure and amnesia. “I’m not looking for answers,” she told ARTnews. “But for some kind of physical proof that things really happened, that they’re not just in our memories.”.

Rosales’s 2024 sculpture Has the myth been shattered encases that infamous yellowed newspaper in a nearly six-foot-tall aluminum frame fitted with a two-way mirror, illuminated by colorful LED lights. Though it resembles a doorway, the work offers no passage; instead, viewers face their own reflections superimposed over the 1992 text, along with photographs of palm trees and police. The temporal distance between then and now collapses onto a single plane, leaving Scott’s question perpetually suspended in the present.

Recent findings suggest that the work also lends its title to a just-opened exhibition at the Broad in downtown LA. Organized by assistant curator Jen Vanegas Rocha, the presentation brings together works by more than a dozen artists spanning six decades. Recent acquisitions by Rosales and Hank Willis Thomas appear alongside art by Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, Glenn Ligon, and Robert Longo, among others. Across prints, paintings, drawings, sculpture, and tapestry, artists appropriate text and images from various forms of public record, drawing attention to the ways media shapes perception of major sociopolitical events. Seen together, the works undermine the assumption that exposing injustice inevitably leads to redress. “There are echoes of the present in the past,” Willis Thomas mentioned. “So is the past present or is the present past?”.

It has been revealed that the Broad’s founding director, Joanne Heyler, sees that unease as central to the exhibition’s timeliness. “The notion of a linear progression of change unfolding in a dependable, escalating way,” she said, is “becoming harder and harder to believe in.”.

According to recent reports, consider the oldest work in the show, Andy Warhol’s Race Riot (1963), in which police dogs attack Black civil-rights demonstrators in Birmingham, Alabama. In 2026, the decades-old image calls to mind the police response to the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd, as well as the more recent pro-Palestine and anti-ICE demonstrations nationwide, in which protestors were often battered and tear-gassed. Warhol lifted the photograph directly from a visual essay by Charles Moore in Life magazine, translating the confrontation into a monochromatic silkscreen. Adopting the incendiary rhetoric of contemporary news coverage, he labeled the peaceful demonstrators “rioters.” Race Riot reflects the artist’s own reckoning with the contradictions at the heart of American life: His obsession with celebrities and mass consumption give way to the sensationalized images of death and violence that belie it, like the mangled cars and electric chairs that also feature in his “Death and Disaster” series. Viewers are left to consider whether the relentless circulation of violence sharpens public outrage or gradually dulls our empathy.

For Willis Thomas, Warhol’s Birmingham silkscreen paintings function as “postcards to the future.” By transforming them from documentation to works of art, Warhol has made a case for their continued relevance. Nearby, Willis Thomas’s photo-based Black Survival Guide, or How to Live Through a Police Riot (2018) revisits the same era to recover another history largely omitted from public memory. While researching the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, he discovered a typewritten pamphlet offering practical advice to Black residents of Wilmington, Delaware, during the nine-month National Guard occupation in 1968. Onto retroreflective vinyl, Willis Thomas printed excerpts from the pamphlet—advice on how to staunch bleeding or communicate during a power outage, for example—atop archival News Journal photographs of confrontations between armed soldiers and the city’s Black communities. Installed in a darkened gallery, the black-and-white images are invisible until a flash of light illuminates them. Rather than merely encountering the past, the audience actively aids in its recovery. “In some ways the observers become the researchers,” he said.

Histories of state-sanctioned violence and resistance movements similarly converge across a nearly eleven-foot-wide canvas in Mickalene Thomas’s 2021 mixed-media painting The Charnel House (Resist #5). Reworking Picasso’s 1944–45 masterpiece of corpses heaped beneath a table made in response to news footage of liberated Nazi concentration camps, Thomas collages photographs and placards from the Civil Rights and Black Lives Matter movements with the modernist’s fragmented anatomical forms. A poster advertising the Black Panther Party’s free breakfast program appears beside a portrait of Angela Davis and the names of Freddie Gray and Alton Sterling, both killed during encounters with police. Here, grief and trauma are paired with resistance and community building.

Recent findings suggest that the language of dissent assumes a subtler register in Ligon’s Narratives (1993), a suite of nine sepia-toned etchings that mimic the ornate typography and florid prose of 19th-century slave narratives. Ligon replaces accounts of enslavement and escape with details from his early education at a predominantly white private school, his desire for other men, and the circumstances of his career as an artist. In his hands, a literary form that freed Black people used to demonstrate their humanity becomes a medium for contemporary self-portraiture and self-determination.

Recent findings suggest that museums, of course, too, play a role in shaping public records. Over the past five years, the Broad has acquired work by 26 artists previously unrepresented in its collection, many of whom are of a younger generation and, like Rosales, actively working in LA. Heyler sees these acquisitions as part of an ongoing effort to better reflect the multiplicity of the communities that surround the institution. “We’re not telling one story but many,” she noted. “We’re always striving to strengthen the connective tissues between them.”.

The exhibition offers an opportunity to showcase many of the newly acquired artists and to extend an art-historical conversation that Heyler traces to exhibitions like “A Forest of Signs: Art in the Crisis of Representation,” a landmark 1989 survey at the Museum of Contemporary Art, just across the street. Bringing together works by 30 American artists, from Jeff Koons to Jenny Holzer, that show examined the unstable boundaries between reality and representation in an increasingly media-saturated society. But the terrain has evolved, Heyler noted. Where artists of that period often exposed the ideologies concealed by authoritative and commercial imagery, audiences today, immersed in social media and generative AI, navigate what she called a “stew of falsehoods and truths.”.

Industry observers note that even so, curator Vanegas Rocha hopes her exhibition inspires something more generative than cynicism, in which artists can be seen as the “architects of better futures.” She locates the potential for systemic change in the power of an individual aesthetic encounter. “It can teach you about the world, about others, about yourself,” she noted. “That single moment can have a ripple effect, leading to a collective difference.” Rosales, likewise, hasn’t relinquished hope. Citing José Esteban Muñoz’s 2009 queer theory book Cruising Utopia, she described hope as an ever-receding horizon that we must continue to endeavor toward. “We are a people that don’t give up,” she said, noting that her mother also took her to protests from an early age. “Standing up for each other, even when you don’t see it right away, does pay off.” Progress, she suggests, may not be linear or inevitable, but that doesn’t make it an illusion. In her mirror, the unresolved question—“Has the Myth Been Shattered?”—is cast back onto the people who might yet determine the answer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.).

Recent findings suggest that nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

According to recent reports, older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

According to recent reports, since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

According to recent reports, in 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

It has been revealed that showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

Recent findings suggest that you can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:.

If you’re newly introduced to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

It has been revealed that don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.
  • Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely fresh, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”.

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing upcoming energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he said.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”.

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez noted, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

The studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its upcoming owners live today,” he mentioned.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez remarked, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”.

He also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

Industry observers note that lisa Marei Schmidt, the director of the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, is leaving her post to take over as director of the Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern, Switzerland, starting August 1, 2027. She will also chair the management board of both institutions and be responsible for their artistic direction. The Renzo Piano-designed Zentrum Paul Klee holds the world’s largest collection of works by Klee, while the Kunstmuseum Bern is Switzerland’s oldest fine art museum.

Schmidt has been at the Brücke-Museum since 2017 and has orchestrated many exhibitions, including Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019), Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22), and Confiscated and Forgotten: The Female Artists Targeted by the Nazi ‘Degenerate Art’ Campaign, which opens April 30 to July 25, 2027. The Berlin museum is currently exhibiting Swedish Modernism until February 28, 2027, with a focus on the artist groups De unga (The Young Ones), De åtta (The Eight) and the Gothenburg Colorists. “To me, museums are places where art and people meet. They provide space for encounters, new perspectives and dialogue across society,” said Schmidt, in a statement on Thursday. “I very much look forward to getting to know the two remarkable institutions, the teams and the people in the City and Canton of Bern. Together, I hope to build on the Kunstmuseum Bern’s and Zentrum Paul Klee’s distinctive qualities and shape their future development.” Related Articles Artist Tracey Rose Accuses Swiss Museum of Censoring Video Referring to 'Muslim Holocaust' Art Recovered in $400,000 Colorado Theft, Portland Museum Picks Architects for $100 M. Expansion, and More: Morning Links for January 10, 2023.

According to recent reports, schmidt was chosen out of 97 candidates who applied for the position. Jonathan Gimmel, president of the umbrella foundation of Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee, said in a statement that Schmidt brings “remarkable professional expertise, international experience and a deep understanding of people” as she shapes the next “development phase of our museums.”.

Industry observers note that before joining Brücke-Museum, Schmidt was a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and a curator at the Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. She studied art history and modern German literature in Marburg, Amsterdam, and Berlin before graduating from the Royal College of Art.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice Newly introduced-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.
  • Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.
  • The organization has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice Newly introduced-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The organization has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate.

Architecture practice Latest-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

Just off this space is a cosy snug that’s been painted a warm ochre hue. It’s separated from the lounge by a custom-made curtain that design studio House of Quinn made from earth-toned fabric offcuts.

It has been revealed that holloway Li is behind the design of the interiors. Instead of doing a through-and-through overhaul, the studio instead aimed to develop a “circular economy aesthetic that felt warm, domestic and low-impact”.

“That ambition aligned with Mason & Fifth’s own sustainability agenda and allowed us to explore how historic buildings like this can be retrofitted in imaginative and progressive ways,” noted the studio’s creative director Alex Holloway.

In each of the guesthouse’s 56 apartments, the bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes in lieu of fitted joinery.

The wardrobes are made up of lightweight timber parts fixed together with metal brackets rather than glue so that, if necessary, they can be unassembled, flat packed, and re-built elsewhere.

Holloway Li worked with Marble Collective to create countertops and splashbacks for the apartment kitchens; all are crafted from limestone that’s been rejected from quarries because of inconsistencies.

The top edge of the splashbacks has been left slightly craggy and unfinished, further celebrating the stone’s natural flaws.

Almost all of the walls throughout the guesthouse have been simply rendered with multi-finish plaster, and any surface imperfections have been left on show.

“In many cases, the most sustainable decision is restraint,” explained Holloway Li’s senior designer Carrie Coningsby.

“Drawing on principles akin to kintsugi and spolia, the approach celebrates intervention rather than concealing it, embedding repair into the visual language of the space,” she added, referencing historic practices focused on reuse and repair instead of replacement.

Mason & Fifth Belsize Park was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects in the running included the winning Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo, which is outfitted with materials salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins, and the London Coffee Factory by Steve Jensen Design, which is structured around a reclaimed timber framework.

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million), or €2,945 million with fees ($3.23 million), at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).

  • Sources indicate that made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek mastos, or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million), or €2,945 million with fees ($3.23 million), at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).

Legend has it that this series of 18th-century porcelain bowls, made by the Royal Sèvres manufacturers, was modeled after the ill-fated French queen’s real breasts. While no documented proof of such a legend exists, the so-called “jatte-téton” or “nipple bowls,” painted in fleshy light pink with an areola and nipple at the tip, do have a surrealistic, convincingly realistic quality, despite a too-perfectly circular shape. Related Articles Auction of Nazi-Looted Torah Fragment Canceled After Outcry and Israeli Government Intervention Can AI Help Identify the Sitters in Historical Portraits?

Sources indicate that made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek mastos, or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC. It is one of four highly prized jatte-tétons delivered that year and in 1788, destined for the royal “pleasure dairy” in Rambouillet, near Versailles, that King Louis XVI gifted to Marie Antoinette. There, per the fashion of the time, nobility would gather to socialize and taste an assortment of fine milk, cream, and cheese delicacies prepared for them.

The rare breast bowl comes from the collection of French dealer Claude Meyer, who passed away in November 2025. His children happened upon it while going through boxes of storage, and learned that their late father, whose Paris gallery closed in the 1990s, had never offered it for sale. It is unclear how Meyer acquired the piece, which is known to have once belonged to the French Marquise de Chanaleilles.

Recent findings suggest that three of the four breast bowls made in 1787 and 1788 for the queen’s royal dairy dishes are housed in public collections today, including two at the Musée de Sèvres and one at the Museo Duca di Martina in Naples. The bowl that sold tonight is the last of that specific series. They are “the most celebrated and the most extravagant shape of the porcelain service,” by the royal Sèvres manufactory for the queen’s dairy, notes the auction house in its description.

Industry observers note that with the bowl comes an intricately carved tripod stand decorated with goat heads in relief, as seen above. Indeed, the breast bowls require a pedestal to hold them upside down, as it were, so as to contain the milk and cream they were meant to serve.

Speaking to Le Journal des Arts about the bowl, auctioneer Alexandre de La Forest Divonne observed: “It has become something of a symbol of the queen; it is truly a totem.”.

The world’s leading architects and designers from over 40 countries joined to celebrate Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, announcing this year’s winners at a party in London.

More than 550 guests from countries including Angola, Canada and India, as well as Japan, South Africa and Uruguay, joined Dezeen for the event at the historic Royal Opera House in central London.

Guests were welcomed with a champagne reception provided by exclusive drinks partner Veuve Clicquot as they entered the Grade-II listed Paul Hamlyn Hall at the opera house.

The hall’s glazed interior was illuminated and washed in vivid colours drawn from this year’s awards graphic identity in a show design led by Hingston Studio.

Partygoers enjoyed their drinks set against a textile softwall bar backdrop designed by Stephanie Forsythe and Todd MacAllen for Canadian studio Molo, known for its sculptural space partitions, furniture and lighting made from paper and textile.

Dezeen’s co-CEOs Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li opened the evening’s ceremony. They welcomed Dezeen’s founding director and board member Rupinder Bhogal to the stage to lead a tribute to the magazine’s founder, the late Marcus Fairs, in honour of its 20th year.

After guests joined in a toast, Hobson and Li then introduced the evening’s keynote speaker, Norman Foster.

The British architect delivered a speech that explored creative and artificial intelligence within the evolving landscape of global architecture. Drawing on his prolific career, the nonagenarian advocated that meaningful innovation requires challenging the status quo.

Dezeen’s editorial director of special projects Max Fraser and awards and events director Claire Barrett then led the evening’s winner announcements.

First to be confirmed were the design categories, which saw design project of the year awarded to the V&A East’s wayfinding scheme.

Stockholm-based Simon Skinner and British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori were named as this year’s emerging designer of the year and designer of the year, respectively.

Skinner and Ilori won in this year’s Designers of the Year initiative, which recognises the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

Recent findings suggest that interiors project of the year, sponsored by Gaggenau, went to Barcelona-based Raul Sanchez’s renovation of an old sailor’s home. Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was awarded emerging interior designer of the year, with Tokyo-based Keiji Ashizawa taking the award as this year’s established designer. The interiors project categories were also sponsored by Programa and Framery.

Architecture project of the year was awarded to Daichi’s treetop sauna. The architecture project categories were also sponsored by Michelmersh and Sanderson.

The evening’s presentations culminated with Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect Elsa Escobedo jointly winning emerging architect of the year, while world-renowned practitioner Lina Ghotmeh was named architect of the year.

All the winners received a bespoke trophy made from sustainably harvested cork produced by Portuguese manufacturer Corticeira Amorim.

Dezeen Awards winners, VIPs and invited guests continued celebrating into the early hours at an exclusive afterparty sponsored by creative technology studio Made by On at the House of Louie‘s sequestered cocktail hideaway, the Alligator Bar.

All Dezeen Awards 2026 winners were published on Dezeen last Monday evening. Each winner was also featured on a dedicated page on the awards website.

The photography is by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery.

Industry observers note that dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology manufacturer Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that that maxim is borne out in “Threads of Heritage,” a retrospective of more than 80 works at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts in Almaty, Kazakhstan.
  • Rooted in traditional Kazakh textiles, her practice is also shaped by the influences of modernist painting and music, moving fluidly between abstraction and figuration and in turn, defying easy categorization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that how does an artist sustain five decades of artistic production while remaining faithful to her cultural heritage? For Batima Zaurbekova, one of Kazakhstan’s most respected artists, the answer seems to be an unrelenting commitment to her craft. “You can’t be lazy,” the 80-year-old artist told me during a recent conversation.

Recent findings suggest that that maxim is borne out in “Threads of Heritage,” a retrospective of more than 80 works at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Her largest exhibition to date, it features the textiles she is known for as well as drawings and paintings. Curated by Alina Fedorovich, a curator at the Museum of Moscow, the exhibition traces a career in which tapestry becomes both a repository of cultural memory and a vehicle for artistic reinvention. Related Articles 3,600-Year-Old Bronze Age City Discovered in Northeast Kazakhstan Carroll Dunham Calls His Filthy Formalism "Abstraction with a Hard-On".

Rooted in traditional Kazakh textiles, her practice is also shaped by the influences of modernist painting and music, moving fluidly between abstraction and figuration and in turn, defying easy categorization. Her tapestries hold seemingly disparate influences, transforming traditional motifs into a distinct visual language. Ornamental Rug (1969), for example, revives motifs associated with horses, spiritual symbolism, and petroglyphs depicting mountain goats. Completed just after her graduation and the earliest work in the exhibition, Ornamental Rug provides a recognizable reference to the country’s landscape via the distinctive horns of the wild argali, a local mountain goat, while distilling these forms into rhythmic, stylized arrangements. The work’s title foregrounds the relationship between ornament and abstraction, suggesting how decorative forms can become a vehicle for modernist experimentation.

Zaurbekova grew up in the mountainous Zhambyl region of Kazakhstan, where textile-making was part of everyday life. She remembers watching older women create syrmak, traditional felt rugs, and kurak-korpe, patchwork quilts meaning “stitched from scraps.” Neighbors gathered to work, sing, cook, and share food, embodying the Kazakh tradition of asar, in which a community joins forces to help a household undertake a task, be it making a carpet or building a home.

In a recent development, textile-making was as much a social practice as a technical one, transmitting skills and cultural knowledge across generations. This collective spirit is evoked in In the Yurt (1985), a weaving in which a maternal figure presides over the dastarkhan, the table prepared for guests. The yurt, a traditional felt dwelling associated with Kazakh nomadic life, becomes a symbol of hospitality, family, and belonging. Its ornaments merge with the surrounding figures, establishing a visual language equally rooted in the formal and the domestic.

In her youth, Zaurbekova had alternative ambitions for herself. “I really loved music, so I wanted to become a musician,” she recalled. However, her seamstress mother encouraged her to pursue painting instead. She is equally accomplished in oil painting and tapestry, and occasionally the same image is translated in both mediums.

Nevertheless, music has remained central to Zaurbekova’s life and practice, in which her visual compositions are animated by repetition, variation, and rhythm—the basic structure of music. This way of working is best observed in one gallery showing three works, each titled Composition and made in 1980, 2019, and 2024. Their stained-glass aesthetic, contrasting color planes, and rhythmic linear forms evoke Henri Matisse’s celebrated “Jazz” series. Undulating figures and vegetal motifs merge within an ornamental field, dissolving the distinction between figure and ground.

“Threads of Heritage” is being exhibited in dialogue with the museum’s collection of Kazakh decorative and applied art. Traditional felt objects, carpets, and ornaments establish the historical context out which Zaurbekova’s work emerges, while the installation reinforces the relationship between inherited forms and contemporary expression. Here, custom-built walls reference the architecture of the Khoja Ahmed Yasawi Mausoleum, an key historical monument whose forms recur in the artist’s imagery, like the monumental Antiquity (1993). The display also evokes the balbal, ancient stone monuments that connect contemporary life with earlier cultures.

The exhibition’s largest gallery showcases Zaurbekova’s technical mastery and evolving visual language. Each tapestry offers a dazzling array of color that boggles the mind. How, exactly, does she coax such subtle gradations from a seemingly limited collection of threads? “Selecting the right colors is a major part of the work—and it takes me a long time,” Zaurbekova explained. During the Soviet period, artists often dyed threads by hand, painstakingly creating transitions from darker to lighter shades. Although commercially produced threads from Belarus expanded her palette in the 1990s, Zaurbekova has continued to experiment, combining those threads and ones she has dyed to create colors all her own. “Kazakhstan, our land, is very rich, and this is represented in the rich colors of my work,” she told me.

Zaurbekova’s textiles are woven over several weeks to multiple months, and the artist still works for up to 18 hours a day. The vertical threads form the foundation of a given work, she explained, while horizontal threads of different colors construct the image. Through subtle variations in their combinations, Zaurbekova achieves tonal effects that can make woven surfaces appear almost painted. She is also deft at making alasha, a traditional yet simple Kazakh carpet.

Recent findings suggest that rather than presenting national identity as a fixed collection of symbols, her compositions transform familiar motifs through color and pattern. In keeping these traditions alive, Zaurbekova said she thinks “all of my work reflects our nationality and national pride.” Kazakhstan (1977) depicts themes of agriculture and collective labor. To make it, Zaurbekova used threads sourced from a Kazakh carpet manufacturer, working within the limitations of an existing palette to achieve subtle distinctions of tone. Her exacting yet delicate manipulation of the threads’ colors gives the woven surface a gentle vibration and shimmering quality. A work like this makes visible the precision and patience necessitated by such a craft.

Industry observers note that A centerpiece of the exhibition is Vastness (1975), a large tapestry from the museum’s collection showing a bride associated with spring and Nauryz, the celebration of the spring equinox and fresh year. Around her, women gather at tables and a young man on horseback appears among the birds. Elsewhere, figures emerge from the surrounding forest, creating a dense tableau that feels as abstract as it is narrative. The exhibition’s final gallery focuses on the shanyrak, the circular wooden crown at the top of a traditional Kazakh yurt. A symbol of home and family, it serves an architectural motif representing womanhood. In Mother Earth (1984), connections between generations of women evoke the continuity of life and inherited knowledge. Zauberkova’s achievement lies not only in her sheer technical mastery, but in her ability to reinterpret Kazakh textile traditions through a vision that is unmistakably her own, creating work that is deeply rooted in its cultural origins while remaining formally inventive and alive.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by José Hevia.

Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a “modern translation of the old wells” used by local laundry workers.

The home is located on Barcelona’s picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients’ clothes.

Raúl Sánchez Architects, which won interiors project of the year at this year’s Dezeen Awards, turned one of the old laundry houses on the street into the two-storey Casa de las Lavanderas.

The house is now home to a couple and their newborn baby.

The lower level of the 80-square-metre building was partly underground and very dark, leading the studio to look for fresh solutions to add more light.

“Since the ground floor is semi-basement, the area furthest from Aiguafreda Street was darker, so to bring light into it, I incorporated this lightwell topped with a skylight,” studio founder Rául Sánchez told Dezeen.

The lightwell also functions as a “modern translation of the old wells” that used to provide water for the laundry workers.

Casa de las Lavanderas faces two streets – Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers – and has entrances on both sides, with the Calle Aiguafreda entrance sitting 1.5 metres lower than that on Calle Granollers.

From here, one flight of stairs leads down to the lower level and the Calle Aiguafreda entrance, and another up to the house’s upper level.

The 40-square-metre lower level houses an open-plan living, dining and kitchen area, a bathroom and a small study.

This can be partitioned off from the living space using folding doors made from wood and rice paper, inspired by the clients’ time living in Japan.

In the kitchen, Sánchez said he added a mirror-clad island to “introduce a sense of fragility without disrupting the open feel of the space”.

The upper level, meanwhile, houses the home’s bedrooms and a bathroom. The two floors are connected by the Klein-blue lightwell, which has oculi on all four sides to help distribute the illumination from its skylight throughout the space.

Sánchez wanted to “bring that picturesque atmosphere of Aiguafreda Street into the house, making it part of its surroundings by reclaiming that well – now translated into a lightwell that also helps regulate the home’s temperature.”.

This was one of many tailor-made solutions to turn the former laundry house into a home.

“There were many challenges, both technical – access to the mezzanine level, the newly introduced staircase, the structural reinforcements – and functional, like fitting the program into just 80 square metres,” Sánchez remarked.

His studio also worked with materials that would complement the existing ones, using terracotta tiles on the ground floor to extend the traditional exterior clay paving and adding colored glazed tiles to the washbasins and bathroom walls.

“Ultimately, the goal is always to create a cohesive, overarching project that addresses all these challenges and offers something extra – something almost hard to put into words, but that translates into simply feeling good in the space,” Sánchez concluded.

Rául Sánchez Architects is right now working on the final phase of the project, the design of its orchard and garden, which will begin at the start of 2027.

The studio also recently designed a concrete home with a sunken courtyard in Cala Tamarit.

Architecture team: Nerea Moya, Marta Gámiz, FlaviaStructure consultant: Diagonal EstructurasEngineering consultant: Mares Engyniers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners rapidly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

According to recent reports, locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

It has been revealed that have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

Sources indicate that it might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates swiftly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”.

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

It has been revealed that also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will rapidly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

It has been revealed that FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

It has been revealed that remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

Sources indicate that you might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that “I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said.
  • Industry observers note that the spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I thought it best to confess up front that I was still forming an opinion about his work. Carroll Dunham took that like a gentleman. He is familiar, he made clear to me during ourranginginterview, with the two main camps of interpretation about his potty-mouthed paintings and drawings: 1) that he is a high formalist with an ear for the unconscious seldom rivaled since Surrealism, and 2) that he is a simple vulgarian.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said. “I made the paintings. They can say whatever they want.” At 76, Dunham is thin, likable, and frank. He has a sharp, deadpan face framed by transition lenses and Beckettian white hair. When we spoke in his studio in Connecticut, he wore a silk suit in the shade of gray-green the French call caca d’oie, the shirt buttoned only in the top half, cholo style, with chunky sneakers in the same shade. Related Articles Some Collectors Feel 'Energized,' Some 'Burned': As the Curtain Rises on the New York Fall Season, Mixed Signals from Market Insiders Dealer Matthew Brown More Than Doubles His Los Angeles Space with Move to Hollywood Media District: 'I Really Believe in LA'.

Industry observers note that the spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants. It was July, and Dunham was between two capstone surveys of a long career. A show of his drawings spanning 1974 to 2024 had recently come down at the Art Institute of Chicago, while curators at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, were finalizing a survey of his paintings from 1983 to the present for December. It was the kind of summary moment an artist is lucky to be alive for.

Since the ’90s, Dunham’s best-known pictures have starred carefully framed cartoon penises, vaginas, and anuses in varying states of specificity, usually attached to the bodies or the faces of humanoids engaged in sex or violence. This scenery belongs to a tradition of ridiculous bodily extremes, from Greek vases to Thomas Rowlandson to Gustave Courbet to Nicole Eisenman. His style, meanwhile, belongs to the black outlines and dropped-in colors of cartoons. That graphic clarity seems to ask us to read his bodily subjects loud and clear, without any of the technical seduction of peers like Lisa Yuskavage or John Currin.

Although his loud and lusty scenarios committed no real transgression (Peter Saul took care of that in the ’60s, then Robert Mapplethorpe in the ’80s), what may genuinely surprise the uninitiated is the academic remove that characterizes the writing about Dunham. His work is discussed—and discussed primarily by those born before 1975—almost exclusively in the specialist language of form or space or paint application, with little reference to the subject matter. It seems that the writers in Camp 1 understand the shock factor that attends men dildoing their rectums with pistols, or angrily ejaculating on each other from enormous penis-noses, as ammunition against the claim that subject should dictate one’s opinion of a painting. As if to deny the charge of prudery, some of them describe moments of rapture. On a Dunham painting made between 2006 and 2012, of a giant woman spreading her anus and vagina above a landscape like a parade float, the artist Paul Chan wrote of feeling transported: “When I entered the room where it hung [at the Whitney], I gasped. The painting was at once exuberant, provocative, and entrancing. It literally took my breath. I promptly glanced at the other people in the room. Was anyone else having an asthma attack looking at this?”.

Representing Camp 2 are John Yau (The Brooklyn Rail, 2007: “Saul is an iconoclast and Dunham is a wannabe.”) and a young man in a basketball jersey I met at the Chicago show. This man was examining a pencil scribble from 2020 of a fist clasping an erection, the balls parted and meatus shaped like a teardrop. I asked him what he thought, and he stated, “I feel like I’m being pranked.”.

Recent findings suggest that dunham walked me to the “other studio,” a smaller room reserved for painting, where acrylic tubes lay neatly on a table in gradients, labels down. A canvas he had just finishedstood on sawhorses. It demonstrated a man with long black hair down on all fours in a sculpture studio. The painting is called Looking for Something, and its protagonist’s pants are on the floor. His skin is white, and a woman, who is purple, kneels behind him, her head thrown back in a wail or moan. With her hand, she does something to the man’s ass that is not visible to us. In the foreground, another purple person, a Peeping Tom, watches them through a window. Nine of these most recent “Sculptor” paintings, from about Covid to now, were to go up at the Matthew Brown gallery in Manhattan in September as a sort of appetizer for the Miami show.

I asked where these recent purple/white folks come from. “They come from my work,” Dunham explained. “And I don’t mean that to be glib. They really do. So to even answer that question, I would have to go, ‘Before I was doing these paintings, I was doing these paintings, then these paintings,’” he continued, miming with his hands successive leaps into the past.

BORN THE FIFTH IN A line of Carrolls to a Connecticut poultry farmer who turned to real estate, Dunham went to Phillips Academy (Andover), class of 1967. The sculptor Mel Kendrick was his roommate. “Tip was doing Rapidograph drawings,” Kendrick recalled as we spoke by phone, using Dunham’s nickname. “Almost hippie drawings, very fine sketches.” (Of “Tip,” Dunham stated, “It’s a WASP thing.”) Kendrick also recalls Dunham’s appetite for science fiction. (Face-down on his studio table, I spotted James L. Cambias’s Darkling Sea.) Dunham took darkroom classes. In the school’s literary magazine, his finely exposed photograph of a pouting and rotund lady in a playground swing illustrates a poem by Anthony Grafton, the historian-to-be. “Anything he did, he always had a touch,” Kendrick said. “Tip is very specific. And that’s something I don’t know if people know about his paintings, even now.”.

After a year at the University of Rochester, Dunham followed Kendrick to Trinity College, in Hartford, where they worked in a small studio art department. “That meant smoking a lot of dope and reading Artforum,” remarked Dunham. On weekends, Dunham and Kendrick would drive down from Connecticut in Dad’s (Carroll IV’s) pickup truck, Kendrick recalled, to sample the new galleries in Soho—Bykert, Paula Cooper, Sonnabend, OK Harris—and to feast on spaghetti and jug wine at the apartment of their Trinity teacher Terence LaNoue.

In a recent development, laNoue made almost three-dimensional combine paintings with poured latex and molds. He “was a great teacher, but I always had a kind of resistance to what he was making,” Dunham remarked. “And I’ve been that guy. I know that I’ve had good experiences between students and me where it really didn’t have to do with them being that turned on about my work.” Dunham never followed, either, in the footsteps of the artist with whom LaNoue installed him for a formative internship. Dorothea Rockburne produced—and still does, at 97—large, clean panes of paper or vellum, lined geometrically or coated in graphite. But the two got on, and still do. “Brighter than almost anybody around,” Rockburne said of him by phone.

What attracted Dunham was the planning implied by Rockburne’s planes—she taught him and Kendrick “how to handle a T-square and other basic things,” she mentioned. He was also drawn to the repetitious text paintings of Mel Bochner (who lived with Rockburne), and to the heaps of raw material arranged by Barry Le Va and by Richard Serra. On graduating, he moved into a loft on Thomas Street shared with Kendrick and Peter Wheelwright, the architect. His 1970s and ’80s in Latest York were “isolation lite,” he told me. Dunham was part of no scene, he said, but befriended the photographers of the so-called Pictures Generation, and married one: Laurie Simmons. For seven years he worked in a frame shop, then for another seven at Time magazine, as a layout artist, all the while plotting his entrance into the art world.

DUNHAM’S ’70s ART BEGAN with single-line squiggles on canvas or paper. Some are elegantly coiled springs, while others resemble long strings dropped to the floor, their loops filled with ground colors of fast-drying casein or acrylic. He debuted with them at Artists Space in 1981, the Chicago survey was their first time on view since. Rockburne sees little of herself in Dunham’s famous later work. “It had that kind of [Sol] LeWittian, instructional aspect,” noted the artist John Newman, another Dunham confederate from those days, by phone. “In the ’70s, drawing was sort of raised to a fresh place,” Newman explained, “as a much more immediate and idea-oriented kind of territory that wasn’t so laden with the history of painting and sculpture.”.

The string-loops soon became blobs. When Dunham found the lid of a shipping crate on the street, around 1980, and used that for his surface, the almost sculptural grains and knots of the plywood veneer became guidelines for even more specific and conflicting blobs all mashed together—amoebas, geysers, wilting donuts, kinked tubes, beans, ripples, Froot Loops—in palettes ranging from medical textbook to clown paint. It is with these plywood paintings that the Miami survey begins. From 1984 to ’88, they appeared in three shows at the Baskerville + Watson gallery, with the middle show limited to monochromes.

“When the veneer things came out,” Newman recalled, it was amazing. “Think about the first time you ever read James Joyce. You really had to step up to it, participate in it. It was fresh information.” The art dealer David Nolan “hated them” at first, he remarked by phone: “I thought these garish, psychedelic colors were just there to shock me, and I just wasn’t interested.” But after a while, he began “to peel away the layers and see how they’re put together. And once I understood that, I thought, Oh God.”.

The third show sold out before even opening, scoring acquisitions by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney, and the Brooklyn Museum. Dunham quit his magazine job. Gestural painting had been deemed safe again by young galleries, and although Dunham used a brand of biomorphism that didn’t quite fit with the headliners—Basquiat, Baselitz, Schnabel—he was made. Instead of buying up pallets of plywood and sticking safely to what worked, however, Dunham pivoted again. By the ’90s, his veneer paintings migrated to stretched linen, this time as single forms. They began to elongate into screaming fish-lipped mouths, nugget bodies, wincing faces, and undeniable penises. “They weren’t until they were,” Kendrick said of these organs. Nolan noticed them, too. But since they were untitled, Nolan said, “I thought he was avoiding what was right in front of our noses. They are bodily explosions. Come on.”.

Recent findings suggest that DUNHAM HAD BEEN PLENTY aware. He described the ’90s work to me as “abstraction with a hard-on.” But he seemed as bewildered as I about its origin. He spoke with plainness about sex and aggression as if he were a social worker, treating his own work as a sort of passive conduit for those realities. This tone did not seem to me like an act. I asked if he had tried to be provocative with his art, then or now. He stated no: “It doesn’t interest me very much … The entire enterprise was provocative.” He spoke of Duchamp’s urinal.

According to recent reports, into the newly introduced century and his large survey at the New Museum in New York from 2002 to 2003, which was his last show of that scale until this year, his canvases begin to carry entire buildings and shiploads, colonies and planets full of hateful little nugget people with their penises, guns, and hideous gourd breasts. The exceptions from sex—lumpy tree scenes and landscapes—became the transgression. From there, he went more humanoid. In the past 20 years, his nuggets have grown up, first into suited G-men with fedoras and angular suits, then into cleanly clarified cartoon nudes, their globe buttocks outlined in elegant black and set in plain landscapes or rooms. They wrestle, fight, bathe, masturbate, copulate, and blind each other. They examine their gaping anuses, their major labia like bike tubes, and their nipples like air-hockey pushers.

It has been revealed that these characters occupy about half the Miami paintings. In one, Horse and Rider (My X), 2013–15, a woman holds her arms up in a “Why me?” pose on the back of a horse. The lines of her reach continue south into a stand of flowers and a broken tree branch, dividing the canvas into a perfect X, which Dunham has left visible in pencil beneath the paint. At the geometric center is the woman’s anus, as if to say “Look here.” Just beneath, the horse’s anus gapes, too. He turns back at us with a look like “Excuse you.” (No human or humanoid, however, has eyes in a Dunham work.).

According to recent reports, dunham stated of this X composition, “I was very excited when I figured out that that would work.” He explained: “It’s two layers of truth. There’s the subject and whatever that requires to be plausibly rendered.” (He counted “breasts, genitalia, asshole, some notion of limbs, and hair.”) “Then the geometry of the canvas has this other kind of truth, and the two things have to become one thing.” And the woman? “I honestly do not remember why I thought it would be interesting to put a woman on a horse in the paintings.” He thought. “It’s nice to have a black dot in the center of a painting. And it’s even nicer when that black dot is a woman’s ass, you know?”.

In a recent development, nolan was the only one I spoke to who saw strategy in Dunham’s turn to hyper-figuration. He saw the artist “dealing with his own demons or faults about the world.” But he described the work as Dunham did, composition-first. “If you try to forget there’s a face in there, the compositions are very strong.” He advised me to view the paintings upside down, pointing out convincing similarities to Aztecan decoration and adding that recently he, Nolan, had refused to sell one—for a lot of money—until the potential buyer flew to New York to see the shapes in person. “That is a problem with the younger generation. They will lose all of the subtleties.”.

In a recent development, WHAT DOES THE YOUNGER generation think? The Miami show this winter (and the Chicago catalog forever) will give them the chance to see Dunham’s career as a single entity and to decide if the evolution of blob to aggression to anus stands up to the hindsight of a more literally minded era. In the purple alien characters on view at Matthew Brown this fall, from the series Dunham calls “Studio on Another Planet” (2022–26), one was hard-pressed not to read a narrative about artists at work in a culture that will misunderstand them: a solitary white male surrounded by voyeurs (critics? dealers? posterity?) as he quietly molds his clay on their land, incurring their sinister attentions. In the last of those canvases, Finished (2019–2025), the aliens have had enough. They’ve dragged the artist outside and are now quartering him to death.

“You’re not supposed to get it,” Newman stated of Dunham’s pictures. “Art is about having an experience.” Newman speaks, Darwin-like, of Dunham’s characters emerging from the primordial soup of the plywood paintings. “Younger people probably don’t know the early work. And I actually think if they did, it would help them understand his later work better.” In my conversations with Camp 1, I began to wonder if there has ever been a generation more permissive, more game, than the one that had Dunham as a sort of living symbol of egress: out of the hermetic tasks of Minimalism, through pure shape, into a future where human fictions of any extreme can live without excuse or embarrassment. And I began to envy them.

According to recent reports, I asked Dunham if he believed pure abstraction existed. He remarked yes, adding, “And I think that when I started my work, I was doing it. And then I think at a certain point I realized that it fascinated me to try to add some really literal aspects of just being a human being incarnated, or incarcerated, however you think about it, in a body.”.

Industry observers note that but I didn’t fully buy Dunham’s hermetic account of his own work as “always in some way self-referential.” There seems to be plenty of lived Artist v. World in his pictures and posture, and plenty of visual breadcrumbs leading to the culture at large. I asked, for instance, which cartoons he watched with his two children, who were born in 1986 and ’92. His eyes widened. “Ren & Stimpy was good,” he mentioned of John Kricfalusi’s unhinged and influential program. “But the masterpiece of ’90s cartooning as far as I’m concerned was Angry Beavers,” which he watched with his son. I was fishing. The affinities between Dunham’s ’90s work and the prevailing depravities of Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network are inarguable; and in those affinities, a fresh generation may see homage to the last golden age of a truly transgressive child-absurd.

Sources indicate that speaking of his younger child, Dunham flashed back: “He came into my studio a lot. He would pick up on things I was drawing and then he would draw stuff of his own that was kind of like that. So I got a lot of, you know, 6- and 7-year-old energy coming back at me about my own work.” Dunham smiled. “It definitely encouraged a certain kind of energy. It’s very sweet to think about actually.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dame Rachel Whiteread, who was the first woman artist to win the Turner Prize in 1993, has been selected to design the 2027 Brit Awards trophy.
  • Sources indicate that the trophy will be bestowed upon musicians nominated for the prestigious award ceremony taking place on February 27, 2027.
  • Recent findings suggest that whiteread said she also agreed to design the statue in an effort to safeguard arts and culture, which she described as being “under very real threat.” “The Brits have celebrated musical creativity and artistry for decades now.

Dame Rachel Whiteread, who was the first woman artist to win the Turner Prize in 1993, has been selected to design the 2027 Brit Awards trophy. The trophy has previously been designed by the likes of Damien Hirst, Zaha Hadid, Es Devlin and Anish Kapoor.

Sources indicate that the trophy will be bestowed upon musicians nominated for the prestigious award ceremony taking place on February 27, 2027. Each trophy takes inspiration from the image of Britannia, a tall, elegant female figure that personifies Britain. For her design, Whiteread has inverted the statue, exposing its silver lining with punched holes throughout. “I exposed the interior of the statue—as an artist would do with their music,” said the artist in a statement. “I accepted the invitation to design next year’s Brit Award trophy, as I saw this as a natural extension of my work—to continue to celebrate and recognize British art and creativity, and to have an opportunity to apply my own perspective within such an iconic British cultural institution.” Related Articles Nnena Kalu Wins Turner Prize, Becoming First Learning-Disabled Artist to Take UK's Top Art Award Rachel Whiteread's Collaboration with French Silversmith Company Inspired by Corrugated Cardboard.

Recent findings suggest that whiteread said she also agreed to design the statue in an effort to safeguard arts and culture, which she described as being “under very real threat.” “The Brits have celebrated musical creativity and artistry for decades now. We have some fantastically creative musicians who have produced music that lays their souls bare, provides hope in times of darkness, or speaks directly about a moment in time,” she added.

Recent findings suggest that in designing the trophy, Whiteread joins a prestigious list of other artists who have given the statue new life: Dame Peter Blake, Tracey Emin, Vivienne Westwood and Yinka Ilori. In 1997, Whiteread became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale, and in 2001, she became the third artist to have her work placed on the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square, which took the form of an inverted resin recreation of the plinth.
