Breaking: London Museum brings "back a bit of London's heritage" with Smithfield Market opening

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.
  • Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London’s history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner.
  • According to the London Museum, it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Hufton + Crow.

Architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.

Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London’s history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner.

According to the London Museum, it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.

Ten years in the making, the opening of Smithfield General Market marks the first phase of the London Museum’s relocation from the Barbican Estate’s former Museum of London, which is set to be demolished.

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have overhauled the General Market, which fell into disrepair after it closed in the 1990s, and will also convert the adjacent 1960s Poultry Market, which is expected to open in 2028.

“There’s an opportunity to represent London as it is now and in the future, and really take city museums to another level,” noted London Museum’s Newly introduced Museum Project director Alec Shaw.

“We’re bringing back a bit of London’s heritage – one building that has not been seen or encountered for at least 30 years, and the other one an amazing architectural gem that hasn’t been fully appreciated and will now be,” he told Dezeen.

The main entrance to the London Museum is marked by a covered street, West Poultry Avenue, which doubles as the Real Time gallery that stretches between the General Market and Poultry Market.

Entering the transformed Victorian market, visitors pass a museum shop and an auditorium before entering Our Time – an expansive gallery illuminated from above by an oculus.

Shops that once wrapped the perimeter of the market trading floor were removed to open up the space, but the restoration was designed to retain hints of the building fabric’s history.

“You can see pockets in the brickwork walls where joists of the first floor and little plaster columns were originally located,” said Julian Harrap Architects partner Lyall Thow.

“There was a second floor, represented by a darkened band where we didn’t overly clean the brickwork, and fireplaces in the upper offices were taken out, restored, and put back where they would have been originally.”.

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects overhauled 42 individual shops that formerly encircled the General Market into 12 multi-storey units.

Six units were kept to contain a restaurant, galleries and learning spaces, while the other six were left for the museum to invite partner institutions to occupy.

“What the ‘museum of tomorrow’ will be is not just a single institute, but a coral reef of small institutes that can plug in – Dezeen could have an office here, a leather upholsterer might have a craft workshop here, restaurants and pop-ups…” remarked Khan.

“This living ecosystem, which is reflective of the city, is possible because of this market building we’ve moved into,” he continued.

“What we’ve done is make openings, windows, and cuts through the floor and ceiling, which allow that energy to emanate out of the city and for the city’s energy to emanate inwards,” added Khan. “At the centre of it all is this enormous public space, the General Market ground floor, where anything can happen.”.

A staircase takes visitors down to London’s Roman street level, to the museum’s permanent Past Time exhibition, which displays precious artefacts.

The restored brickwork walls in the subterranean space are interrupted by a six-metre window, revealing passing Thameslink trains.

A series of underground vaults that were discovered during the museum’s construction will open to visitors in spring 2027.

“This museum epitomises the idea of the primordial reflex in us to dig to find various treasures,” remarked Stanton Williams co-founder Paul Williams.

The architects aimed to make the qualities of the existing spaces work to the museum’s advantage, displaying delicate objects in the underground gallery and maintaining the communal feel of the market space on ground level.

“Decisions based on the building – like precious objects should be kept underground because it’s got a greater thermal inertia – loosen the straitjacket around the museum having to act like a museum in other spaces,” said Khan.

“It means some other spaces can be more market-like and have a more public-facing potential that a normal museum wouldn’t be able to do,” he continued. “The building has enabled the museum to become a different kind of museum.”.

Unisex toilets were designed in a Victorian style, with decorative tiles depicting wildflowers that grew in London’s bombed-out sites.

Elsewhere in the museum is a 24-hour cafe where original interior tiles and a timber staircase were restored.

Shaw hopes the London Museum will be an inviting place that residents and tourists want to return to time and again.

In a recent development, “We want to be super welcoming – we don’t want to be intimidating as a museum,” mentioned Shaw. “Some of the other museums are quite imposing buildings.”.

“We want to be a destination, not just a museum, but a place for people to keep coming back to.”.

Other museums recently completed in London include V&A East by O’Donnell + Tuomey and the V&A East Storehouse by Diller Scofidio + Renfro, which was given a Dezeen Award for its wayfinding design.

Photography by Hufton + Crow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.

Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.

“We believe it is crucial not to impose a common consistency across our projects,” Kuma told Dezeen.

In a recent development, “Every project is unique, shaped by a one-off combination of site and client. Preserving that uniqueness requires an open mind. Personally, I rapidly lose interest when things are planned in advance.”.

“That stated, there are certain topics, many of which are shared by our generation, such as feminism, the care for natural resources and a shared public space, that interest us on a personal level, and I imagine they find their way into our work,” added Escobedo.

“We try to approach them with a sense of joy.”.

Although they have already designed a wide range of projects, from installations to houses and public toilets, the duo would like to work on more varied schemes and unusual projects, along with completing their own, long-running renovation.

“It would be nice to actually finish this self-renovation project at some point…” said Escobedo.

“More seriously, I’d love to experiment with the reuse of materials on a larger scale, or in a European context, working with European craftspeople.”.

“I would love to work on overlooked building types and uses, especially those that have little place in architectural history and attract few expectations,” added Kuma. “Designing a toilet pavilion for the Expo, a building type that nobody expects to become architecture, is one example.”.

Along with the variety in projects, both architects agreed that the wide range of daily activities is what they most enjoy about being an architect.

“The variety, the diversity,” mentioned Escobedo, when asked about her favourite part about being an architect.

“One day you’re on a construction site with incredible Japanese carpenters, the next you’re discussing a detail with your favourite thermal engineer, the following week you’re taking part in a conversation with colleagues you admire, before finding yourself struggling to install the plumbing and tiles in a shower because you had the brilliant idea of taking on a self-build project.”.

Kuma also added that he enjoys the intensity of working on site.

“The construction site,” he mentioned. “Nothing is more stressful or demanding, with all the struggles involving people and money. Yet every time I see a building taking shape, I feel glad I chose architecture. There is something addictive about it.”.

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning studio Kuma&Elsa, as described by the duo:.

Nakano House, Tokyo, Japan, 2026.

In a recent development, “The client’s childhood home, a traditional Japanese house, has an engawa gallery open to the garden. The new residence occupies the top two floors of a building owned by the client. She, along with her two sons and their families, will move into three apartments located on the sixth and seventh floors.

“At the centre of each apartment, we inserted a hut-like volume that gathers the quieter rooms: a small living room and the bedrooms. In the space carved out around it emerges an intermediate zone – an engawa that serves both as a place to stay and as a passage.

“Balcony, engawa, and hut thus form three spatial layers that resonate with the childhood home. The structure consists of Y-shaped modules made of lightweight steel sections and bracing cables, typically used in shelving systems.

Industry observers note that “These modules are arranged two by two in mirrored pairs along a regular grid, with occasional inversions. From these fresh dwellings, one can look down across the street at the engawa of the childhood home. This project does not seek to nostalgically replicate that memory-laden place, but rather to build a new home nourished by the memories of the old one.”.

“One water is a bathing and rest pavilion for the Osaka World Expo 2025. Toilets are at first glance a pragmatic facility, dedicated to human physiology. But they are also intimately linked to contemporary problems such as the use of natural resources and gender.

“One water uses the path of rainfall on the accessible roof and its subsequent accumulation to create encounters between water and the public, and contribute to the supply of the toilets.

“The design of the pavilion allows for the reuse of materials and structural components, and makes no gender distinction in the toilets, because, after all, ‘we are all fish in one water’.”.

House by the temple, Saitama Prefecture, Japan, 2024.

“The house is opposite the entrance of a temple that is surrounded by a park of ancient trees and a wall, as if it belongs to another world. Reflecting this closed composition, we designed the house as an everyday world for a family.

“The main building is located at the back of the plot and has a quarter-circle initiative to reduce its own shadow. The street facade is a single-storey hut, which creates a continuity between the open space of the park and the garden of the house.

“On the ground floor, the park is the backdrop to the house. On the first floor, each room offers distant views of the temple, like an observatory.”.

Yamada House, Fukuoka, Japan, 2020.

“A daily public space in a residential area. We create a plaza in a small residential area where human life is still at human scale.

Recent findings suggest that “The house is like the background that forms the square. The composition consists of various couples: the smooth black mortar of the outer wall and the rough crushed black basalt ground, the emerald entrance hut and the crape myrtle tree with white flowers, the interior spaces and the outside square.”.

Water Flower Courtyard, Montpellier, France, 2019.

It has been revealed that “The life of a flower is short: we wanted to express the fragility of a concentrated life from flowering to dispersal. This project was open to the public for a week during the Montpellier architecture festival Festival des Architectures Vives in June 2019.

“Eighteen lightweight units made of two-millimetre-thick aluminium sheets are laid out together as a forest.

In a recent development, “The tube is a vase that contains water and peony flowers, the bowl contains water and slate stones. All structures are self-supporting and their stability works as in a roly-poly toy. After a few days, petals start falling on the surface of the water.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.
  • Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down.
  • Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Sources indicate that have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

In a recent development, when your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

In a recent development, have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a significant part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

According to recent reports, some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

Recent findings suggest that for infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Sources indicate that another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health concerns that need medical attention.

Recent findings suggest that dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

Industry observers note that while liver challenges can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Burberry.

Fashion brand Burberry‘s chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum, made from “memories, traditions and little treasures.”.

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA’s) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

Recent findings suggest that “This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?” Lee said. “It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me.”.

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.

The tree, which was made as part of Burberry‘s 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.

According to recent reports, according to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from “memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook.”.

Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

“We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual of dressing the tree,” she said.

“I’m always drawn to work that’s handmade, and Ann is a master of her craft,” Lee said of the collaboration.

As well as the tree, the V&A will also be showing The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon, a display that traces the history of the trench coat. Burberry has a multi-year partnership with the museum and is set to open The Burberry Gallery at the South Kensington location in 2028.

Lee has previously unveiled an archive-inspired logo for Burberry, and a few years ago, the brand revealed its redesigned London flagship store.

Photography courtesy of Burberry.

#229155. Industry News: Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1476 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1476 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, photography by Cyril Marcilhacy.
  • Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.
  • In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, photography by Cyril Marcilhacy. unless stated.

Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.

Having only graduated in 2025 from a master’s in architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – for which he was awarded the Arthur Rotch Prize for highest overall mark – Kpodo is already someone Lokko believes will “help shape the next chapter of African architecture”.

Kpodo’s work, which sees him blur the roles of architect, artist and archivist, is focused on revealing what he calls the “silences” in prevailing narratives about Ghanaian architecture, and challenging the idea that Ghana’s future development must be a “linear prescription of urbanisation”.

If this sounds theoretical or speculative, Kpodo’s approach is anything but: the site of his MIT thesis was an almost five-acre stretch of farmland in Ghana to which he purchased a 99-year lease in 2022, and is presently using as a live site to consider alternative forms of development in the region.

Stating how, if nothing else, the purchase would “preserve the value of the money I had in my savings account,” Kpodo sees the site becoming an alternative institution of sorts, constructed using materials he has salvaged from vernacular buildings that would otherwise be demolished.

In a recent development, “The committee at MIT was a bit shocked, because they weren’t used to the idea of a thesis project existing in the real world,” Kpodo told Dezeen. “But I still thought of it as almost as a sort of sketch, just at 1:1 scale.”.

“Doing that gives you something to test – people are going to interface with it; you can test out its failures and success very quickly.”.

Growing up in Kumasi, Kpodo initially focused on visual art in school before pursuing a course in architecture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), and subsequently MIT.

At KNUST he was promptly exposed to narratives around both architectural success and Ghana’s own architectural history that left him seeking something more “homegrown”.

“We had a lecture from Francis Kéré in which he spoke about his Serpentine Pavilion, and how taking on commissions from big institutions or big clients can become critical for defining your practice,” said Kpodo.

I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the substantial commissions to come?

“At the time, I couldn’t imagine any of these commissions coming to those of us working in the South. I couldn’t see any architects who were operating on that scale, or even at a kind of global scale,” he continued.

Industry observers note that “It almost had the opposite effect on me. I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come? I think it’s by being local that I can have something to offer to the world.”.

Kpodo became interested in local architectural archives, initially those of the KNUST Development Office, but also the less formalised collections of images and drawings that he encountered online.

He soon helped establish Postbox Ghana, a research collective initiated by artist Manuela Nebuloni to create an alternative architectural archive using postcards and stamps from the 1950s to the 1980s, which often depicted examples of Tropical Modernism and state infrastructure constructed following Ghana’s independence.

However, Kpodo still felt that these archival materials did not speak to his own understanding of Ghanaian architecture, having grown up in a “not-so-well-to-do context” in Kumasi and only really encountering modernist architecture when first entering the KNUST campus.

According to recent reports, “The whole archive that I was exposed to, whether it was in the Development Office or in the postcards, had a huge, significant gap in it,” he said. “I remember stories my dad would tell me about building practices and cultures that just didn’t make it into this archive or our training in architecture school.”.

According to recent reports, “As a newly independent country, Ghana wanted to break away from any kind of ethnographic notion of what the ‘Gold Coast’ – to use its colonial name – was. So those ‘traditional’ buildings and other forms of practices did not make it into the framework of thinking about what our future meant,” he continued.

“But even though these buildings are far removed from the city centres and from the archive, they were foundational in the sense that they enabled the cocoa industry, and brought in the money that built the institutions and structures that are enshrined in postcards.”.

Kpodo began to photograph these vernacular buildings himself, many of them farm structures made using laterite, a type of local red earth that is formed into air and sun-dried blocks for construction.

When I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’.

Upon finding many of these buildings slated for demolition, Kpodo has more recently begun to purchase them, before carefully deconstructing their laterite structures to become the raw material for new structures on his land.

The idea was initially met locally with some confusion. “I remember one man said, ‘oh, are you going to extract gold from the walls?’ because laterite can contain gold,” he recalled.

“But when I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’ And then some kids would even begin making their own proposals. For me, just creating that imagination is worth it.”.

The land that Kpodo purchased in 2022 is in Ghana’s eastern region, and was at the frontier of cocoa production in the early 1900s. Some descendants of the first farmers on the land are still based there, and were among those Kpodo interviewed to understand the history of the landscape.

Alongside the widening of a communal path – the focus of his MIT thesis – and the moving of vernacular building materials there, he has also constructed a simple timber deck, both as a rest point for the farmers and an observation point for watching future changes unfold on the site.

Industry observers note that if I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too. You can only do so much in an exhibition setting.

Kpodo envisions that this future will include both newly introduced agricultural processing facilities for the farmers on the land, as well as community spaces that enable further discussions around its ongoing development.

Recent findings suggest that this work also forms the basis of Kpodo’s educational and curatorial work. He is keen to continue “speaking both languages” – the more practical with the conceptual – but he feels the latter should always be grounded in a “local base” rather than detached from it.

Industry observers note that in 2023, his work with Postbox Ghana was exhibited at both Vantage Point Sharjah and the Venice Architecture Biennale. In 2025, he curated the LagosPhoto Biennial alongside Maria Pia Bernardoni and Robin Beth Riskin, with the theme of Incarceration.

Kpodo also taught on the one-month Nomadic African Studio at the African Futures Institute, founded by Lokko as a space “dedicated to rethinking education, culture, and practice from the African continent outward.”.

Most recently, he orchestrated the transportation of the wall of a laterite farmhouse a little further afield to the Fondation Cartier in Paris, as part of the exhibition Ibrahim Mahama: Harvest Season, where it is accompanied by images from the Postbox Ghana archives.

“If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too,” he noted. “You can only do so much in an exhibition setting. You can only talk so much. If the work has no ground and no local base, then I think it becomes very difficult for you to bridge what it is that you’re presenting versus the work that it proposes to be doing.”.

“We need to cultivate other sites that do the real work, sites that translate it into something which is not necessarily concerned with an educated audience,” he continued.

“My sense is that we’re increasingly going to see the most ‘powerful’ institutions seek out these hyper-local narratives and projects as a way to really understand the world.”.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

Photography by Cyril Marcilhacy. unless stated.

Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy.
  • At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll.
  • According to recent reports, in a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting customers’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

According to recent reports, in a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

It has been revealed that some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

On top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He states this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

Industry observers note that on top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

Sources indicate that “We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” indicates Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”.

Sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

In a recent development, “During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu says. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu notes. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

It has been revealed that but GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, says Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.).

According to recent reports, at the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu states losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

Recent findings suggest that as mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

It has been revealed that “Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she says. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying complications may benefit sexual health.

That means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

According to recent reports, “Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he says. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.).

Sources indicate that GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, says Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, claims board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

Of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a recent development, in a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

It has been revealed that A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist users stated the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

Recent findings suggest that “Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he says. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”.

Recent findings suggest that for those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon notes. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

Sources indicate that in these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

“Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer says. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”.

Sources indicate that desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer says. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec states, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”.

Industry observers note that if you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

In a recent development, working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

"Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.
  • Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.
  • It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Iwan Baan.

Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

“My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,” mentioned Richter.

It has been revealed that “The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips,” he continued. “Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”.

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project’s context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a “profound culmination of many years of [Richter’s] research into abstraction”.

“I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind,” she stated.

“This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness,” she continued.

“The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience.”.

Inside, Richter’s paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and upcoming works made especially for the pavilion.

Among the fresh works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.

The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

According to recent reports, elsewhere, Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing. In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf noted that “what matters is I know why we did things”.

Photography by Iwan Baan.

#229150. What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

📅 10 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1510 w)

What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live.
  • I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a newly introduced wellness trend making the rounds on social media.
  • Sources indicate that there’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a newly introduced wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

Sources indicate that there’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz indicates.

According to recent reports, it seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

It has been revealed that I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

Fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” notes Fertz. “You are born young.”.

It turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

Sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky says. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”.

At school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

In a recent development, research reveals that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

Sources indicate that “I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”.

Even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

In a recent development, italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

“Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”.

Paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very key to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

It has been revealed that at cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

Sources indicate that in fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in Newly introduced York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert indicates. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”.

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

The antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

In Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

“Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo states. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”.

Recent findings suggest that indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

It has been revealed that italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

According to recent reports, “The most key thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz notes. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, strategy outings, and get out of the house.”.

According to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz says, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:.

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she states.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach fresh situations in life.”.

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is vital here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:.

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina indicates it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most key planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina states gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she indicates it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she states.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina indicates.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A collection of showcases, old and new, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events. Dezeen’s US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings.

The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of NYCxDesign, revealed that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.

The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.

While BDNY and high-end showcase Salon Art + Design have always been held in November, other design fairs have sprouted to take advantage of the opportunity to show during this busy period.

The week is positioning itself, without any explicit organisation, as a massive event in the Upcoming York design calendar.

Even NYCxDesign, still scheduled for May as usual in 2027, held a November event bringing in designers Ross Lovegrove, Karim Rashid and Rem D Koolhaas for a talk moderated by Upcoming York-based design writer Camille Okhio.

The panellists spoke about the potential for AI and derided the inclusion of craft in conversations about design. However, as writer Debika Ray noted in an opinion piece for Dezeen, crafted, one-off pieces have lately come to dominate design indicates.

NYCxDesign staking out a talk with well-known industrial designers suggests that its May event could be devoted to industrial design, while November complements it with a focus on collectible furniture.

This was definitely true this year, when collectible designs dominated the November showcases.

In a recent development, among these was the Brussels-founded design fair Collectible. For its third Newly introduced York iteration, it moved from office tower-turned creative hub WSA to a former movie theatre on the Upper East Side that is being developed by entities related to WSA.

While the space fit the experimental nature of the work, the execution was, by some accounts, somewhat chaotic, with one exhibitor staff member being sent to the hospital after an unstable light fell onto her head as the exhibitors were installing it in their booth.

Collectible called it an “isolated occurrence involving an exhibitor’s equipment”.

“The safety of our exhibitors, staff and visitors is a priority, and we take any reported incident seriously,” a representative for Collectible told Dezeen.

“Collectible maintains safety procedures for the fair and expects all exhibitors to ensure that their own equipment is installed and secured appropriately.”.

However, the fair also had some strong showings. Philadelphia-based Dudd Haus showed a pared-down booth with its usual mix of conceptual one-offs. Particularly of note was a milled-aluminium floor lamp by Jordan Maurice and a paravent made with telephone cords by Overt Cove.

Also eye-catching was a booth of droopy glass lamps and shades with erotic overtones by Upstate Latest York gallery Freaks, and another sensual booth with drapes and lacquered furniture by Iitem studio.

Industry observers note that the fair’s scenography carried the sleek, modern, USM-laden feel from the prior additions. Curators Alex Tieghi-Walker and Lynette Nylander designed special sections.

Bas-reliefs were popular on otherwise modern furniture, including a battened screen by Polish studio Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki for Objekt Gallery and a coffee table with raised ceramic on its base by Small Things Studio for Salon 21.

At Collectible, Montreal design collective Ensemble showcased its members’ work on nooks in a wall made with USM panels.

In a recent development, this was just a taste of what Ensemble had in store for the week. The collective brought their signature experimentation to Yabu Pushelberg’s Tribeca studio, creating a plywood room-within-a-room to showcase work, including newly introduced lamps by Zebulon Perron, sculptural glass lamps by Alex Joncas, metal works by Jérémy Paguet, leather lamps by Jeta Studio and brass-lined mirrors by Jeremy Le Chatelier.

It was an extremely focused showing that proved sometimes you can do more with less.

At Salon Art + Design, a few younger galleries stuck out from the historical work and ultra-high-end designs that usually characterise the fair.

Brooklyn-based Zarolat’s showing included ash-wood lamps with cellulose shades by Natural Urbano and Polybion, while Newly introduced York-based hub for Brazilian furniture, Bossa Furniture, showcased a greatest hits of mid-century São Paulo makers, including Joaquim Tenreiro.

Sources indicate that BDNY was, as usual, where most of the actual commerce took place during the week. While the interior designers and architects descended on the sample-forward showing, a few brands showed stand-out collections, including Sancal’s showing of Júlia Esqué’s playfully fringed armchairs and Santa & Cole’s modern, fun lighting.

Later in the week, LA-based Basic Space, run by the organisers behind Design Miami, returned to SoHo. With artistic direction by Alexander May, the stark, white-cube approach differed from the in-situ, multi-room afair that characterised the first New York Basic Space in 2025.

The fair featured a focus on major names and multiple co-curators competing for attention on the promotional materials and in the execution.

Standout pieces included the live-edge wood furniture with small metal connective elements by Brooklyn-based designer Gregory Beson, as well as Daniel Swarilov’s metal credenzas, in a section curated by Marquel Williams.

In a recent development, paris-based Harry Nuriev created a metallic take on first-class airline seats as a standalone installation. Another booth featured an oversized sofa by NFL player Stefon Diggs’ luxury furniture brand Si Vis Pacem, illustrating the fair’s mix of design with celebrity culture.

Finally, Mexico City-based creative studio Fábrica, run by artist Darryl Richardson and partner Maryah Ananda, held its La Sala showcase in a loft near Penn Station.

With a focus on international Black designers, the showcase featured art and design, with the space shaped like a living room by interior designer Johnathan Bailey.

Furniture pieces of note included a slim metal chair by Kai Avent-deLeo and an armchair by Mark Grattan.

The social focus of the event gave it an aesthetic heft, and a few of its stated goals, “community over curation” and “warmth over spectacle”, made it stand out from many of the other offerings from the week.

Judging by the willingness of the different fall fairs to join in, it seems likely that the November design week will fully take off.

The Ember-01's metallic chassis is paired with a transparent glass panel, showing the internal circuitry and a bitrate-reactive RGB light inside. It's very cool, but there's more to it than that.

The Ember-01 also comes with a 10-band PEQ, through the Aful app. This theoretically will allow you to alter the sound of your music to exactly what you want, which is pretty exciting.

If you're still looking for some headphones to go with this dongle, check out my list of the best-sounding wired headphones at any price.

In a recent development, equipped with physical media buttons, a dedicated hardware gain switch – which literally blew my mind – and in-line microphone support, the Ember-01 aims to bridge the gap between everyday smartphone use and audiophile performance. Though for the sake of total transparency, early impressions have suggested that its ambitious software features still need a bit of polish.

Under the hood, the Ember-01 pairs its AKM AK4493SEQ DAC with a CB5100 Pro USB bridge, supporting high-res playback up to 32-bit/768kHz PCM and native DSD512, alongside UAC 1.0 compatibility for gaming consoles...

Recent findings suggest that in English, that means it uses high-end audio chips to convert digital files into ultra-crisp, studio-grade analog sound, supporting virtually every ultra-high-resolution music format around. And that's while also including a compatibility mode so you can plug it into gaming consoles like a Nintendo Switch. Hoorah!

Its 3.5mm single-ended port outputs 125mW (and supports headset microphones), while the 4.4mm balanced output ramps things up to a massive 500mW into 32 ohms with a 121dB dynamic range.

A major selling point for me is its built-in 10-band Parametric Equaliser (PEQ), offering customisable frequencies, gain, Q-values, and digital filters. However, early testers have reported launch-day limitations, including the Android app not being properly ready at release, leaving users reliant on a web-based desktop interface.

However, once Aful get this fixed, I can see this being a popular bit of kit for audiophile on the go.
