    #229058. How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

    📅 19 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1566 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

    How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

    📅 19 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.
    • But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects.
    • The research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone concerns, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.

    But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects. And a recent study that just garnered a bunch of attention raised the possibility of new ones.

    The research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone concerns, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones). The study also found a link between GLP-1 use and heightened risk of gout, a type of arthritis that causes pain and swelling in the joints.

    The lead study author mentioned he became interested in whether GLP-1s might affect bone and other connective tissue after some of his patients “developed serious tendon tears following relatively minor injuries,” according to NBC News. After analyzing five years of medical records from nearly 147,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, the study authors concluded that GLP-1 use was associated with a “significantly increased” risk of osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and gout.

    Recent findings suggest that of course, this news is likely unsettling for anyone on these medications. But should we be legit worried about these findings? And how exactly could GLP-1s harm bone health in the first place? We tapped two experts for answers, along with practical tips for protecting bone health while taking GLP-1s.

    In a recent development, first, some relieving news: As of now, there is “no sound scientific evidence” that suggests GLP-1s directly increase the risk of osteoporosis or osteomalacia, Marci Laudenslager, MD, an obesity medicine physician with The Johns Hopkins Healthful Eating, Activity & Weight Program, tells SELF. (Same goes for gout, she adds.).

    According to recent reports, dr. Laudenslager, who was not involved in the study, points out that it was observational in nature, meaning it looked at correlation…not causation. “While well-conducted observational studies can reveal a potential relationship between a medication and a clinical outcome, they cannot determine whether a medication directly causes that clinical outcome,” she explains.

    According to recent reports, another limitation of the study is that it relied on medical records alone, which means it assumed that all patients who were prescribed GLP-1s, as noted in their medical records, were actually taking the drug. In reality, many patients who are prescribed GLP-1s are unable to take them because of cost or medication shortages, Dr. Laudenslager indicates. Moreover, people who do start taking don’t always continue due to insurance, cost, or problems tolerating the drug, she adds.

    In a recent development, beyond that, the study didn’t take into account factors that commonly impact bone health, like exercise habits, nutritional habits, and other lifestyle factors, Kelyssa Hall, an exercise physiologist and certified strength and conditioning specialist at Hospital for Special Surgery, tells SELF. “These factors can play a huge role in bone health with or without the addition of GLP-1s.” The study also didn’t account for certain endocrine conditions, cancers, alcohol use, family history, and steroid use–all of which can also play a role in bone health, Dr. Laudenslager adds. And the study didn’t note which specific GLP-1 drug people used and the dosage, she adds.

    Sources indicate that lastly, the study findings have not yet been peer reviewed–a step that Dr. Laudenslager describes it as “essential” in the scientific process. As Hall puts it: The study “highlights the need for more research on these topics.”.

    Okay, so that particular study has its limitations. But other research supports the notion that these drugs may be linked with declining bone health. So…is there actual cause for concern?

    According to Dr. Laudenslager and Hall, taking GLP1-s can indeed decrease bone density for some people. But that’s likely due to the volume and rate at which people lose weight while on these drugs—and not anything specific to the medication itself, Dr. Laudenslager says.

    “When you take GLP-1s, there can be rapid weight loss which means there is less load being carried around on the skeleton,” Hall says. “Bone formation or strengthening is improved with load to the skeletal system,” she explains, “so losing weight decreases the regular load on the bones overall.”.

    It has been revealed that over time, this decrease in loading can translate to a decrease in bone density, Dr. Laudenslager indicates. But, again, this isn’t unique to GLP-1s: “Significant weight loss through any mechanism—lifestyle change, medications, or surgery—can impact metabolism as a whole and bone metabolism, in particular,” she says. Basically, whenever you lose a bunch of weight—regardless of how you lost those pounds—there’s always a risk of bone loss.

    In short, while it’s true that some people taking GLP-1s have had changes to their bone health, these changes seem to “be driven primarily by magnitude of weight loss rather than a direct, negative consequence of the medications themselves,” Dr. Laudenslager says. That stated, the use of GLP-1s and bone health “is an active area of study,” she adds. More research is needed to fully understand the impact of GLP-1s on bone density.

    According to recent reports, resistance training is crucial for pretty much everyone—and that includes folks on GLP-1s. One of its many benefits is that it’s been shown to improve bone density, Hall says. That means it can be a helpful strategy to bolster bone health when you’re on a GLP-1. Plus, strength training can help guard against muscle loss that can happen when you’re losing weight. “Retaining muscle mass is important for strength and stability,” she says. And it can also help support your overall metabolism, she adds, which can help your body sustain weight loss results for the long haul.

    Sources indicate that if you’re new to strength training, Dr. Laudenslager recommends gradually building up to a routine of two to three sessions a week, with at least a day off in between each workout to allow your muscles the time they need to recover. Before getting started though, make sure to check with your doctor or other medical provider so they can advise what type of workouts are safe and recommended for you.

    A common side effect of GLP-1s is appetite suppression, which can sometimes lead people to follow a really low calorie diet. Calorie restriction can suppress bone growth and increase the risk of fractures, according to research, which is one of the reasons you want to make sure you’re still eating enough to support your overall health while on a GLP-1. “Hunger is an essential hormonal cue we all need in order to sustain health,” Dr. Laudenslager says. The ideal amount of calories is highly individualized, but if you’re unsure that you’re getting what you need, bring it up with your doctor or another qualified expert, such as a registered dietitian.

    Protein is often touted for its muscle-building benefits, but it’s also vital for bone health, as it helps to build bone mass. The recommended dietary allowance for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilograms of bodyweight a day—a general guideline that Dr. Laudenslager also suggests for people taking GLP-1s. She suggests a slightly higher intake for people at greater risk of bone health issues (such as older adults and postmenopausal women) and lesser amounts in people with kidney disease. Just make sure that as you prioritize protein, you don’t skimp on crucial components of a well-rounded diet, including fiber, water, healthy fats, and essential vitamins, minerals, and nutrients, she adds.

    Rapid weight loss can be harmful for bone health, so to mitigate this risk, strive for a more gradual reduction in pounds. The recommended rate of weight loss depends on your starting weight, but as a general guideline, Dr. Laudenslager recommends losing 5% to 10% of your total weight over the course of about six months. This translates to an average of about 0.5 to 2 pounds lost a week. So if you notice that taking a GLP-1 is causing you to lose weight at a faster pace, bring it up with your doctor. They may want to adjust your medication dosing to help slow your weight loss rate into a more ideal, gradual range.

    It has been revealed that bone loss isn’t an overnight thing. In fact, clinically significant bone loss typically happens over the course of years, Dr. Laudenslager says. “This means there are a wealth of opportunities throughout a person’s weight loss journey to prevent and treat bone loss early on if it’s detected through surveillance.” So if you have any bone health concerns, mention them to your doctor (though hopefully your provider is proactively thinking about this too).

    It has been revealed that on that note, Dr. Laudenslager strongly encourages people interested in obesity treatment to seek care from a board-certified obesity medicine physician. She recommends the American Board of Obesity Medicine and the Obesity Action Coalition websites as resources for finding a board-certified provider.

    In a recent development, GLP-1s can be a true game-changer for people struggling with chronic health conditions. Unfortunately, there’s still a lot of societal stigma and misunderstanding surrounding obesity, including the misconception that “anti-obesity medications are dangerous and should be avoided,” Dr. Laudenslager indicates. In truth, though? “The medication side effects are quite manageable when prescribed by providers who are well-versed in current practice guidelines,” she says.

    #229054. Breaking: For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

    📅 20 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1743 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

    📅 20 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends.
    • Industry observers note that “I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF.
    • It has been revealed that so she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends. Over the course of six months, they watched as she shed 30 pounds, going from 130 back to what she calls her “healthy original weight” of 100 pounds. Even still, her loved ones worried about the extent of her weight loss and didn’t want her to lose even more.

    Industry observers note that “I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF. The 34-year-old, who lives in Montreal, asked to use only her first name to protect her privacy. “I was really tired of trying.” At five feet four inches, she wasn’t obese and didn’t think her primary doctor would approve a prescription.

    It has been revealed that so she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed. Immediately after starting Wegovy, she claims, “the weight started coming off incredibly fast.” After six months she decided she wanted to stop. But as soon as she got off Wegovy, the weight came back: She gained 10 pounds in a month. “I realized, I can’t stop,” Caroline says.

    In a recent development, so for the past six months, she has been taking Wegovy again, this time at a maintenance-level dosage. But there’s one substantial difference: This time, she’s keeping it a secret from her boyfriend and family. “Now that we’re talking about kids, he’s seen all the impacts [of the drug] and he’s done with it,” she states. Since she lives alone, hiding her medication from him is relatively easy—she stashes it in the back of the fridge, since it needs to be kept cold. But she’s still worried he’ll see it, and when they travel together, she has to hide the medication in the hotel room fridge—or, if they’re visiting his parents, in their refrigerator. “So imagine, I’m hiding stuff in my parents-in-laws’ fridge, hoping they won’t see them,” she says. “It’s super awkward.”.

    In a recent development, caroline isn’t the only woman going to great lengths to keep her GLP-1 use a secret. On a recent thread on the r/GLP1microdosing subreddit, women shared their tips and tricks for hiding medication from their partners. One stashes them in a tomato paste box. Another uses a play food container from a child’s pretend kitchen. Still others have turned to an opaque feta cheese container, butter stick box, anchovy paste box, empty bottles of women’s probiotics and Alani Nu supplements, a plastic to-go container, a metal water bottle, a box of wine, and a baking soda box in the back of the fridge—all to conceal the weight loss medication.

    It has been revealed that “It’s a real thing,” Kia Mitchell, MD, who specializes in family and obesity medicine, tells SELF. She has seen numerous women in her Jacksonville, Florida, practice go to similar efforts to hide their medication from their partners. The first time she heard about this pattern, it was from a patient who “just didn’t want to turn this into a debate at home,” she indicates. “She just wanted to have the option” to take the medication. “A lot of my patients are similar,” Dr. Mitchell adds. “There’s this loss of control with the gaining of the weight, but being able to control the narrative around weight loss has been empowering and exciting” for her patients. “Because now they can reveal it on their own terms. That’s where the control comes back.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the reasons women want to reveal their weight loss medications on their own terms are palpable in that subreddit thread. “If my husband found out, it would just be a series of lectures,” wrote a user called Vivid-Act-6442. “Just don’t want to hear any negative or critical opinions,” wrote another user called [deleted]. “After 52 years of marriage, one knows one’s mate.” One woman chimed in to say she was hiding her meds from her teens—because she didn’t want them telling her ex-husband. “I just don’t feel like the questions,” she wrote.

    According to recent reports, dr. Mitchell has mixed feelings about this type of secrecy. Anyone on a health journey benefits from having a “network that’s really cheering for you,” Dr. Mitchell says. “Dealing with something like this, I want people to have community.” But, she continues, it’s “empowering and protective” for women to get to decide who knows about their weight loss drugs—even if, ideally, “you really want to be in a relationship with someone you trust completely.”.

    From a medical standpoint, there are some potential pitfalls to hiding GLP-1s from a significant other. For one, it’s easier to get pregnant while taking them—Mitchell notes she has “several GLP-1 babies” in her practice. There are also the drugs’ potential side effects, and hiding medication can make it more difficult for a patient to turn to her partner if she’s struggling. And more generally, secrecy can cause stress. “When someone is trying to lose weight, we want their stress hormones to be as low as possible,” Dr. Mitchell says. “If you’re trying to hide [medication], we’ll be fighting an uphill battle if you’re stressed about that.”.

    The bigger glitch is hiding GLP-1 medications from your regular doctor, something that has become much easier thanks to the rise in telehealth companies like Hers and Ro. That’s a problem Caroline is having: She didn’t tell her doctor both times she went on Wegovy and still doesn’t want to, even though she’s concerned about how the drug may interact with the Accutane and Ritalin she takes. The idea of admitting her GLP-1 use to her doctor makes her anxious, since she doesn’t want to break their trust. But her annual physical is coming up, and her doctor will see that she’s lost a lot of weight.

    It has been revealed that “I use ChatGPT as my doctor at this point since I can’t be honest with my own doctor,” she states. “I say, ‘Hey, this is my actual weight, what type of dosage is okay to take with other drugs?’” Admittedly, she adds, this is “probably not the best option.”.

    Caroline got her Wegovy prescription through Hers. During the process she was only asked for basic bloodwork and received no counseling, just “documentation to read.”.

    Craig Primack, MD, the head of weight loss at Hers, tells SELF that the company’s prescribing doctors “do ask [patients] to talk with their primary care doctor about the care they’re getting.” He acknowledges that the company doesn’t do much in the way of direct counseling but says that “we ask about mental health and anxiety and stresses.” The Hers app contains what Primack terms “psychologist-built information” about topics such as sleep management and eating personas.

    According to recent reports, dr. Primack is “absolutely” aware that some patients hide their medication from their partners. He says that some don’t want to say anything until they’ve proven they can lose weight; some don’t want to say anything because of the medication’s cost; some worry about how it could change the way they and their partner see each other. “Your weight and persona set up a dynamic in your couple,” Dr. Primack says. “When you start changing that, sometimes spouses get very jealous—‘Oh my god, you’re becoming potentially more attractive.’ Not that weight is directly linked to that, but that’s what I hear them say.”.

    Sources indicate that and then, of course, there’s the more general stigma associated with weight and weight loss. “One benefit of telemedicine is it takes the bias and stigma away,” Dr. Primack says. “One reason we are here is because people are uncomfortable going to talk to their primary care doctor about it.”.

    Whether or not Caroline decides to tell her doctor about her medication, she still will have to grapple with the larger issues that her Wegovy use, and her secrecy around it, have raised. “It’s very stressful,” she indicates. “The fact that not only can I not talk about it, but I’m also unable to get off of it. I don’t love the idea of taking medicine like that forever, but I’m kind of stuck with it.” She doesn’t want to gain weight, she explains. “But I wonder to which extent I’m too harsh with my criticism of my body. Maybe my goals are too intense.”.

    Recent findings suggest that given the incredible degree of vulnerability and sensitivity tied up with weight loss, the dilemma about whether to tell people about a GLP-1 medication is all too understandable. But how to tell people can make it easier, says Rachel Goldman, PhD, a clinical assistant professor in the department of psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a clinical psychologist whose areas of expertise include weight management and disordered eating, tells SELF. “Framing it around their own experience and needs can make the conversation feel more manageable and less like something they have to defend,” she says.

    Recent findings suggest that since deciding whether to have this conversation isn’t easy, Dr. Goldman would first encourage a patient to “think about their why,” she notes. “What led them to this decision? What does this treatment mean for their health and wellbeing?” Once someone feels more grounded and confident in their reasoning, “it becomes easier to communicate it with that confidence.”.

    Dr. Goldman also suggests coming up with some sample scripts before having the conversation. “I would suggest that they lead with their own personal experience and not think about others and why/how others are using it,” she indicates. “I would encourage them to use ‘I’ statements.”.

    It’s also helpful to think ahead of time about a partner’s potential reaction and to have a strategy in place for different scenarios. Thinking about what you want from a partner is likewise helpful—is it support, understanding, “or simply space to make their own health decisions without judgement?” Dr. Goldman asks. She adds that it’s notable to remember that a partner’s initial reaction might not be their final reaction—it can take time for someone to process a conversation and to work through their own biases and misconceptions.

    “Ultimately,” she says, “the goal isn’t to have a perfect conversation, but it’s to open the door to more honesty, connection, and support over time.”.

    But if that fails, there’s always a box of anchovy paste.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has unveiled the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre in London, the first purpose-built development to provide temporary accommodation for homeless families in the UK.
    • Situated in the London Borough of Havering, the centre contains 74 flats for families and two floors of community space built around a central courtyard.
    • Forming part of the wider regeneration of Harold Hill Estate, Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre was designed to help alleviate the growing demand for temporary housing in the local borough.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Photography by Fred Howarth.

    Architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has unveiled the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre in London, the first purpose-built development to provide temporary accommodation for homeless families in the UK.

    Situated in the London Borough of Havering, the centre contains 74 flats for families and two floors of community space built around a central courtyard.

    Forming part of the wider regeneration of Harold Hill Estate, Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre was designed to help alleviate the growing demand for temporary housing in the local borough.

    Intending to set a benchmark for temporary family housing in the UK, Hawkins\Brown aimed to create a welcoming building that eases the stress of families facing homelessness.

    “Many of the families who come here are fleeing hugely painful domestic situations,” said Hawkins\Brown partner Nick Gaskell.

    “The Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre aims to make a traumatic period a little more bearable by providing a caring, calming and uplifting environment for as long as they need it.”.

    Designed to be in keeping with the neighbouring buildings, the exterior of the U-shaped building is lined with striped bands of orange-toned bricks and pops of pale green metal sheeting.

    A secure, landscaped courtyard with play space at the centre of the building helps bring natural light into the surrounding flats.

    Inside, the apartments were designed to offer higher-quality living arrangements than typical temporary housing, with tall windows, underfloor heating and open-strategy kitchen, living and dining rooms.

    Community and family support spaces on the ground floor of the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre include a reception, visitor breakout areas, children’s indoor play spaces, communal laundries and staff facilities.

    Based on the studio’s research into dementia-friendly design, Hawkins\Brown used colour zoning, visual landmarks, accessible graphics and high-contrast colours in the centre, aiming to make the space easy to navigate for residents and visitors of all ages and abilities.

    Elsewhere in London, architecture studio HTA Design recently unveiled what it states is the largest latest-build council housing development in the UK.

    In Ukraine, architecture studio Office for Future is working on intends to transform a school into temporary housing for families affected by the war in the country.

    Photography by Fred Howarth.

    #229051. Breaking: Meet Kiki Goti, Kelly Wearstler's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1253 w)
    📖 Baca

    Breaking: Meet Kiki Goti, Kelly Wearstler's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1253 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Next up in Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, which marks 20 years of Dezeen, is Greek designer Kiki Goti, who was nominated by Kelly Wearstler for her innovative approach to ornament and artisanship.
    • Goti has experienced a remarkable rise since presenting a furniture collection made from salvaged foam insulation during the 2023 edition of Milan design week.
    • Her conceptual, research-led work typically explores heritage, identity and craftsmanship, resulting in playful objects and spaces that reexamine the cultural codes embedded in design.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Next up in Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, which marks 20 years of Dezeen, is Greek designer Kiki Goti, who was nominated by Kelly Wearstler for her innovative approach to ornament and artisanship.

    Goti has experienced a remarkable rise since presenting a furniture collection made from salvaged foam insulation during the 2023 edition of Milan design week.

    Her conceptual, research-led work typically explores heritage, identity and craftsmanship, resulting in playful objects and spaces that reexamine the cultural codes embedded in design.

    Goti was nominated as an emerging talent to watch by American designer Wearstler, who praised how Goti “approaches ornament with the precision of an engineer and the instincts of a sculptor”.

    “That refusal to treat craft and technology as opposites is going to matter more over the next 20 years,” Wearstler added.

    As well as a shared love of ornament and the decorative arts, Wearstler also picked up on how Goti’s practice is informed by her background in robotics and machine learning.

    “It’s amazing to be nominated by such a significant designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail,” Goti told Dezeen.

    It’s amazing to be nominated by such a big designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail.

    Goti added that she was pleased to be recognised by a leading female designer, as her creative muses are mostly women and femininity plays a major role in her own practice.

    “My work is very personal so of course there are a lot of references to being a woman,” she said, adding that she draws inspiration from well-known artists and designers such as Louise Bourgeois and Faye Toogood.

    Goti spoke to Dezeen from Paris, where she currently lives with her partner, French filmmaker Vincent Staropoli, having recently relocated there from New York.

    She was raised in Thessaloniki and received a diploma in architecture from the local AUTh university before completing a masters degree in Integrative Technologies and Architectural Design Research at Stuttgart’s Institute of Computational Design.

    The move to Newly introduced York came after accepting a research position at Pratt Institute, but during the Covid pandemic Goti realised that she missed making her own work, so began experimenting with found materials.

    Industry observers note that “I really didn’t know what I wanted to do,” she recalled. “But through my research at the university and the Latest York design community I realised there were other people working in a similar way, which encouraged me to stick with it.”.

    The initial collection was followed by projects made with glass, marble and, most recently, a series of furniture pieces featuring lacquered wooden surfaces that contrast with bell-like aluminium elements.

    The outcomes are very unpredictable. Because the collections all look different there isn’t anything people can point to and say ‘that’s clearly made by Kiki’.

    Goti explained that her work usually starts with research into a specific technique or a material that interests her, before she then applies her findings to the design of an object.

    She stated she finds this approach creatively fulfilling as it offers endless opportunities, though as someone early in her career it means there is no identifiable style associated with her work.

    In a recent development, “I don’t usually have a form or a shape in mind when I start,” she remarked. “So the outcomes are very unpredictable. Because the collections all look different there isn’t anything people can point to and say ‘that’s clearly made by Kiki’.”.

    “In the long term I hope people will recognise my work because of its research-led approach,” she continued. “We need to take more time to understand other artists’ work and not judge everything based on a few images on social media.”.

    Decoration and ornamentation are recurring elements within Goti’s oeuvre, although she doesn’t want to be labelled as a maximalist.

    Industry observers note that “My work is sometimes very ornamental and sometimes it’s more minimal,” she added. “So there’s a gradient and the outcome is really determined by the process.”.

    Like many contemporary designers, Goti does not produce all of her own work, instead utilising a network of expert artisans to help bring her whimsical and deeply personal creations to life.

    “I’m a very collaborative person and I think we can create better outcomes when we put our minds together with other people,” she noted.

    “My architecture background really helped me develop this collaborative mindset and I think one of the key things you learn as you get older is to be selective about who you work with.”.

    I’m a very collaborative person and I think we can create better outcomes when we put our minds together with other people.

    The collection she developed with Marble Sachanas (top) exemplifies this collaborative approach, applying Goti’s visionary and playful style to an ancient material sourced from a quarry close to her home town.

    Goti met the company’s representatives during 2025’s Milan design week and struck up a conversation that led to them returning this year to exhibit the outcomes as part of the Alcova event.

    Projects such as the marble pieces and the furniture she developed for Mexican gallery Toro Manifesto fall into the category of collectible design, which Goti pointed out is a consequence of their artisanal production rather than a conscious decision to make high-end, limited-edition objects.

    “Everything nowadays is so expensive to make,” she explained. “If you want to make something that’s well-crafted you have to pay for the materials, the shipping, the labour and that causes the price to be high – it’s not the designer’s fault.”.

    The armchair, coffee table and sideboard were shown at the Collectible design fair in New York, but Goti stated she would also be interested in working on designs that could be licensed and produced by a brand.

    She is currently developing a collection of glass objects that will be smaller and more affordable than her large-scale Graces vessels, while retaining their exuberant aesthetic.

    Alongside her personal projects, Goti also runs an interior design practice together with Staropoli called The House Special Studio, which combines her distinctive aesthetic approach with his cinematic vision.

    The studio’s first completed project was the renovation of a compact Paris apartment, which reflects their desire to create spaces that feel fun, personal and lived-in.

    Looking ahead to what the next 20 years might hold, Goti intends to continue experimenting with different materials and techniques, while attempting to document her design process in a more detailed and consistent manner.

    She believes some designers, herself included, have reacted to the isolated experience of Covid lockdowns by working more with their hands and exploring latest ways of collaborating, which she hopes will continue over the coming years.

    “I feel we’re all craving crafts and handmade objects more than ever,” she said. “The more digital content we are fed, the more we are drawn back towards analogue experiences.”.

    “I think we all want more physical interaction with materials and with each other, as well as more intimate settings where we can come together and make things. That’s the kind of future I want to see.”.

    Industry observers note that to celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

    #229050. It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

    📅 21 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2315 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

    It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

    📅 21 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day.
    • Recent findings suggest that I have just seen Michael (the newly introduced Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release.
    • It has been revealed that on screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day. The world is suddenly too bright, too loud, and slightly unreal. You have, after all, been inside someone else’s carefully constructed reality for two hours. And then you’re back outside, blinking into the afternoon light, not quite returned to yourself, the movie still clinging to you like perfume. It’s in this particular state that I meet Nia Long for an early lunch in a quiet corner at the Chateau Marmont.

    Recent findings suggest that I have just seen Michael (the newly introduced Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release. I’m still thinking about the film when Long, who plays Jackson family matriarch Katherine Jackson, arrives looking chic but low-key in an oversized blazer, wide-leg jeans, and a Miu Miu baseball cap pulled low. As we ease ourselves into the conversation, I’m struck by the strange doubling effect of the movie vertigo: the woman before me and the woman I have just watched, layered like two transparencies held up to the light.

    It has been revealed that on screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness. The first time we see her, watching her boys rehearse, the frame holds on her loving face for just a few beats. She claims almost nothing. She doesn’t have to. Juxtaposed to Colman Domingo’s blustering portrayal of Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson’s uncanny performance as his late uncle Michael, Long has found a way to make silence load-bearing. Restraint is the most visible thing in any scene she occupies.

    It has been revealed that in person she seems the opposite of restrained. She is blunt but also quite warm, with a dry sense of humor and a deep well of emotional intelligence. She is very much a Scorpio. She notices everything. And, in playing Mrs. Jackson (who is still with us at the age of 95), Long has tapped into the part of herself that knows how to let silence do the work. The word she reaches for when she talks about the experience of playing the matriarch—a word she will return to several times during our conversation—is grace.

    “There have been moments in my life where I’ve been required to be more graceful than I’ve ever had to be in the past,” she indicates. “And that requires a sense of really being able to dig deep into some sort of self-examination. Like, what do I stand for? What’s key to me, ultimately, regardless of Hollywood, the noise? And number one, for me personally, my children come before anything. And so I think when you look at Michael’s journey, and you look at Katherine’s journey, the only way you thrive and survive is through a tremendous amount of grace.” She pauses. “What I think I learned from her is that sometimes grace is really quiet.”.

    Long occupies a place in our cultural memory that few actors do. She is, for a certain generation, the platonic ideal of ’90s Fine, a phrase that’s not only about beauty or aesthetic but also about a certain feeling. Watching her as Nina in Love Jones or Jordan in The Best Man or Lisa in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, you conjure up a place and time and attitude that feels synonymous with Long. Of course, there is the image, and then there is the human sitting across from me, eating her go-to order of salmon with a side of mustard. And as she does, I ask what she thinks about the iconography and the nostalgia that surrounds her.

    “My commitment to work is not for accolades or attention, or even to be famous, quite honestly,” she says. “But I do think because of my commitment to truth and purpose, there is a thing, and I don’t know what that thing is, that people see in my work. And it makes them feel good. It makes them feel inspired. It makes them feel like they know me.”.

    In a fickle Hollywood landscape that’s even more fickle when it comes to Black actors, Long doesn’t take the longevity and love she’s cultivated for granted. “There's highs and lows,” Long admits. “I’m having a great year, but I don’t know what’s happening next year.”.

    It has been revealed that long has starred in several iconic Black films, and she’s always been intentional about how she plays her characters. Much like with the Katherine Jackson role, she creates a version of the person that feels, to her, like something true.

    According to recent reports, “The only strategy I have in this game is my bank account. Let’s strategize how we’re going to make money and create generational wealth. That is where I’m strategic.” She laughs, scratches her palm. “My hand just started itching the minute I said money. That’s a good thing. Maybe something’s happening. Something’s coming.”.

    In a recent development, once she’s in it, though, the work becomes something more personal. “I work hard to make sure that when I represent us, it’s not just someone putting their agenda on me. Whether it’s my hair, my makeup, my wardrobe, my lines.”.

    Now that her eldest son is in his 20s and her youngest son, 14, is old enough to stay home by himself, the actor feels ready to expand in all directions. She wants to continue to produce more films, craft new stories both behind and in front of the camera. She tells me about a new film she’s just wrapped shooting in New York, Don’t Ever Wonder, a romantic dramedy (“If that even exists anymore”) three years in the making. It will feature her onscreen reunion with Love Jones leading man Larenz Tate. Directed by Eugene Ashe and featuring an ensemble that includes Blair Underwood, Susan Kelechi Watson, and Algee Smith, the film is all about second acts.

    Recent findings suggest that “This is not a continuation of Love Jones,” she emphasizes. “This is a continuation of love, and of what happens once you’ve had your kids, they’re off to college, and you’re empty nesters. And that’s kind of where the story begins. There’s a lot of funny and there’s a lot of heartbreak, and I think it’s a really honest story.”.

    It has been revealed that in talking to Long, I get the sense that honesty and truth is what she values most in the stories she tells. It’s what she values in life as well. Perhaps that’s what compels me, somewhere in the middle of our lunch, to unmask. I mention that I am conducting the interview a little out of sorts, having just ended a 12-year relationship.

    “Okay, but when was it really over?” she asks.

    "You didn’t have to gag me like that!" I say.

    She laughs. I tell her that I am trying to imagine what life will look like—what I will look like—on the other side of this break-up. That’s when the idea of grace comes up again.

    It has been revealed that in 2022, Long went through that peculiar part of fame where something private becomes public overnight: her partner’s cheating scandal that resulted in the end of their 13-year relationship. She doesn’t have to go too deep into it if she doesn’t want to, I assure her, but the actor doesn’t shy away. On the other side of the experience with her ex, with whom she now has a healthy coparenting relationship, she has an unflinching clarity about the whole ordeal.

    “The amount of pouring into myself that I’ve done is strong and mighty and intentional. I’ve now identified the things that I need to work on and the things that I need to heal. But I have also identified what is intolerable.”.

    It has been revealed that that clarity has been hard-won. When the cheating scandal happened, there was a groundswell of support from fans, a protectiveness over Long as a woman and as a cultural touchstone. But in the instances that she’s talked publicly about it, including in our conversation, I’m struck by how her gratitude for the support is always tempered with nuance.

    Industry observers note that “I’m proud of myself for giving so much grace. For being able to say people make mistakes and things happen. It’s life. When the stakes are high, the news is significant. I can’t do anything about that, but I don’t have to protect my ego in any of this.” She notes all this very matter-of-factly, which is the only way she seems capable of saying things.

    Recent findings suggest that in the same straightforward tone she suggests I write out everything I need to say to my ex without sending it, because ultimately “it’s not about another person’s behavior. It’s about your bottom line and the magnitude in which you’re committed to self-love,” she indicates. “I don’t think it's healthy to hold onto things because then you’re just walking around with this burdensome energy. It could be writing it down. It could be meditation. It could be prayer. There’s a lot of ways to manage the noise. But you don’t have to respond to the noise with the undercurrent of your own trauma.”.

    I write down this last sentence because it is useful, but also because it is the key to something I’ve been watching Long do across the whole of our conversation: find the lesson in whatever she is given.

    Long is working on her first memoir, a process she describes as one of the “biggest, bravest, challenging” things she’s ever done. It’s been a two-year process, a constant negotiation with her own relationship to letting go.

    “I can read something I wrote two years ago and go: ‘Oh no, that’s not actually how I feel about that now.’” Long’s father, Doughtry Long Jr., a poet who died in 2020, told her the hardest thing about writing is knowing when to stop. “And I’m like: When is that going to happen? Because I haven’t gotten there yet.”.

    The memoir takes her back to Iowa City, where she spent six years of her childhood while her mother attended university. She was born in Brooklyn, in a Trinidadian household where everyone on the block was Black. Living in the Midwest during her formative years, she encountered few other Black girls, which disoriented her relationship to race.

    “In writing this memoir, I realized the impact that experience had on my own view of beauty,” she notes. “And my own self-acceptance of being a pretty brown-skinned little girl growing up in Iowa. I thought I was beautiful because my mother stated it and my family said it, but the world told me something different.” She lets that sit. “So to now be a face for Estée Lauder, it’s kind of ironic, because I didn’t feel beautiful until Black Hollywood said I was beautiful.”.

    That an entire generation of Black women found a reflection of Black beauty in Nia Long while Long herself was still waiting to see it tells us something about how beauty standards work, and how much labor goes into transforming them. Nineties Fine, after all, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a corrective, Black Hollywood’s answer to a century of the larger industry rendering Black women invisible or, worse, making us visible in ways that were wholly out of our control. Long’s most iconic characters—and indeed, Long herself—reflected a new idea of beauty, of the Black leading lady, expansive in some ways and still restrictive in others. Now, some 30 years on, Long embodies a new facet of being a Black woman in Hollywood.

    “Black don’t crack” gets lobbed at Black women constantly, ostensibly as a compliment, but one that sometimes erases the very real pressure that comes with aging—especially aging on a public stage, especially when people have a particular image of you stored in amber.

    It has been revealed that but Long is not interested in pretending that the body is not a thing that transforms. “I’m 55. I got hormonal stuff going. Your body shifts, changes. It’s a whole new body.” She is not wistful about this. She also ate the truffle parmesan fries and does not appear remotely conflicted about it. She mentions the coming press tour for Michael, how she wants to be in beautiful gowns but she also wants French fries.

    Sources indicate that “I don’t deprive myself of anything that I want,” she indicates. “I find the balance.”.

    It has been revealed that beauty was never her primary currency, she says. It had to be something else, other inheritances: her father’s curiosity, her mother’s fierce self-possession. Tattooed and free-spirited, her mother wore leg warmers in the middle of summer because they matched her outfit, and she did not care for one second what anyone thought about that. Embarrassed, Long would beg her mother to take them off. She never did. As an adult, Long sees the power and freedom in that.

    Recent findings suggest that our plates are carted away. Long has to leave soon for a pizza party at home with her youngest son and his friends. Before she goes, I ask her what freedom, at this point, is to her.

    According to recent reports, “Being able to do what you want to do when you want to do it, because it serves your spirit, not what everyone else thinks you need to be or should be,” she indicates. That type of freedom, Long adds, doesn’t require an audience.“You don’t have to have anyone else’s permission to do what you love. And it doesn’t have to be on the substantial stage. It could be in your kitchen. I know I have freedom right now to make a pizza. I’m going to do it.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, this edition of Latin America in Focus explores the ways architecture shapes collective life across different scales and contexts, from public infrastructure and educational environments to the urban histories that continue to inform cities today. The featured projects in Ecuador and Mexico consider how cultural facilities and landscape interventions can support shared activities while responding to their surroundings, while the history of Santo Domingo traces the early development of colonial urban planning in the Americas. The selection also looks at current approaches to cultural heritage conservation and public space, highlighting initiatives in Peru and across the region.

    Public Architecture, Learning Environments, and Civic Life.

    From educational facilities to community infrastructure, recent projects and recognitions highlight how architecture accommodates collective activities and responds to different social contexts. Scheduled to open in December, the 31,000-square-foot Fresh Mexico Literacy Institute by Multistudio and Design Plus Architects brings together flexible learning spaces, reading nooks, recreational areas, and a central courtyard designed to accommodate more than 550 learners and educators, extending educational activities beyond conventional classrooms. In Mexico, COLECTIVO C733 was named the inaugural recipient of the Siza Award for Public Architecture, established by the Serralves Foundation to recognize socially engaged practices working with public space and local communities. The studio's portfolio includes markets, cultural facilities, transport hubs, parks, and public landscapes, among them Matamoros Market, Tapachula Station, and Bacalar Eco-Park, alongside projects developed with SEDATU in vulnerable communities. The award recognizes the studio's contribution to civic infrastructure and public space, bringing renewed attention to architecture's role in supporting shared spaces and community life.

    Related Article Borrowed References, Local Languages: Blended Styles on Latin American Façades.

    Colonial Urbanism and Indigenous Spatial Traditions.

    The Colonial City of Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic offers a historical perspective on the development of urban planning in the Americas, tracing the formation of a settlement that became an early precedent for colonial urban structures across the region. Founded in 1496 and relocated to the western bank of the Ozama River following a hurricane in 1502, the city was reorganized under Nicolás de Ovando around a central plaza, a cathedral, and a regular street grid. Predating the Laws of the Indies of 1573, its layout represents an early example of planning principles later formalized across Spanish colonial settlements, while its two distinct centers around the main square and riverfront reflect the relationship between civic authority and commercial activity. The city's spatial history also raises questions about the influence of Indigenous settlement patterns, with research suggesting that the Plaza Mayor may have occupied the center of an earlier Taíno settlement organized around communal open spaces known as bateyes. This possibility offers another reading of colonial urbanism, in which the imposition of European planning systems may have also involved the appropriation and transformation of existing spatial structures.

    The Floating Cultural Center El Embarcadero / Natura Futura.

    Industry observers note that located along the San Pablo River in Babahoyo, Ecuador, the Floating Cultural Center El Embarcadero by Natura Futura introduces cultural and educational infrastructure to the Barreiro neighborhood, where residents lack access to public social and cultural facilities. Developed with REARC Practice Lab, local organizations, and the community, the project combines a floating cultural center with a floodable amphitheater, an open-air educational ring, and a mobile Canoe Library. Built on an approximately 10-by-16-meter platform, the center accommodates a library, community kitchen, educational spaces, and common areas. Its timber truss structure and split-bamboo roof respond to the local climate, while floating structures, floodable surfaces, and mooring systems accommodate seasonal changes in the river's water level. The Canoe Library extends the initiative to remote riverside communities, bringing books, workshops, and educational activities by boat. Through these interconnected spaces, the project approaches the river as an extension of the city's public realm and a setting for collective learning and cultural exchange.

    Visitor Center at La Hacienda Clase Azul / Elías Rizo Arquitectos.

    Located in Capilla de Guadalupe, in the highlands of Jalisco, Mexico, the 6,625-square-meter Visitor Center at La Hacienda Clase Azul by Elías Rizo Arquitectos draws on the traditional Mexican house and its central courtyard. Set between an agave landscape and an oak forest, the project comprises eight volumes connected by a portico and arranged around a central courtyard with a reflecting pool, forming a horseshoe-shaped plan that opens toward the surrounding landscape. The building accommodates a welcome hall, museum, store, bar, restaurant, and visitor experience spaces, while a basement houses the tequila cellar and service areas. The reflecting pool also provides thermal insulation for the cellar, while subterranean courtyards bring natural light and ventilation to the lower level. Rocks sourced from the site were processed and used throughout the building's walls, connecting its material expression to the surrounding terrain.

    Kaybé Tulum – Multisensory Park / Arquitectura Mixta.

    Industry observers note that located within a tropical jungle in Tulum, Mexico, Kaybé Multisensory Park by Arquitectura Mixta is an 800-square-meter landscape project organized around a sequence of sculptural bamboo structures and winding pathways. Commissioned as part of a low-density residential development, the park preserves much of the existing vegetation, allowing its architectural interventions to emerge within the surrounding landscape. The route connects several pavilions, each exploring different relationships between nature, perception, and the senses, including Toroides, an entrance structure formed by interlocking bamboo geometries; El Átomo, a multipurpose gathering space; and Torre Nikte, a flower-inspired lookout tower with a helical staircase. Bamboo is used throughout in different structural configurations, including laminated beams and woven elements, demonstrating its versatility in creating varied geometries while establishing a consistent architectural language across the park.

    Getty Releases Conservation Project for Peru's 17th-Century Church of Rondocan.

    Industry observers note that the Getty Conservation Institute has announced a multi-year project to conserve the Church of Santo Tomás de Aquino, known locally as the Church of Rondocan, in Peru's Cusco region. The initiative, developed in partnership with the Dirección Desconcentrada de Cultura – Cusco, will address earthquake-related damage through seismic retrofitting and support the conservation of the 17th-century adobe structure and its collection of more than 300 cultural objects. The collection includes religious paintings, gilded wooden altarpieces, sculptures, and textiles, as well as eight paintings by Italian Jesuit artist Bernardo Bitti, a series previously thought to be lost. One of the paintings will be transferred to the Getty in 2027 for scientific analysis and conservation. Construction is scheduled to begin on site in 2027, with the regional cultural authority funding and carrying out the work while Getty monitors its progress.

    Bloomberg Philanthropies Expands Asphalt Art Initiative Across the Americas and Caribbean.

    Bloomberg Philanthropies has opened applications for a new edition of its Asphalt Art Initiative, which offers grants of US$100,000 to cities across the Americas and the Caribbean to transform streets into safer and more vibrant public spaces through art. Up to 10 cities will be selected to develop projects that reclaim street space for pedestrians, improve road safety, and create new gathering places, with technical support from Bloomberg Associates, Street Plans Collaborative, and TY Lin. An updated study examining more than 50 projects across the United States found a 52% reduction in traffic crashes involving pedestrians or cyclists, a 32% decrease in overall crashes, and a 55% decline in near-miss incidents involving pedestrians following the interventions. Previous projects include redesigned intersections in Puebla, Mexico, where average vehicle speeds decreased by 61%. Cities with populations of at least 50,000 can apply until February 11, 2027, with selected projects expected to be implemented in late 2027 and 2028.

    Sources indicate that in 1966, architect and researcher Alexander Kira published "The Bathroom: Criteria for Design", a study that challenged conventional approaches to bathroom planning. Drawing on research into human anatomy, physiology, ergonomics, and personal hygiene practices, Kira questioned whether standardized bathroom fixtures adequately responded to the needs of their people. His work proposed reconsidering these environments through the relationship between the human body and its surroundings, rather than relying exclusively on established dimensions and arrangements.

    In 1966, architect and researcher Alexander Kira published "The Bathroom: Criteria for Design", a study that challenged conventional approaches to bathroom planning. Drawing on research into human anatomy, physiology, ergonomics, and personal hygiene practices, Kira questioned whether standardized bathroom fixtures adequately responded to the needs of their users. His work proposed reconsidering these environments through the relationship between the human body and its surroundings, rather than relying exclusively on established dimensions and arrangements.

    It has been revealed that nearly six decades later, Kira's questions remain relevant. Although technological developments have expanded the possibilities of bathroom design, the fundamental challenge persists: how can architecture accommodate everyday activities while improving comfort, efficiency, and adaptability? Today, part of the answer lies in the integration of technical systems that support both the visible and invisible components of these spaces.

    From Exposed Fixtures to Integrated Bathroom Systems.

    Related Article 5 Design Strategies for Contemporary Bathrooms.

    The evolution of bathroom technology has transformed the relationship between sanitary fixtures, building infrastructure, and architectural surfaces. Traditional floor-mounted toilets and exposed plumbing systems have historically shaped bathroom configurations, with layouts largely determined by the placement of pipes and drainage connections. In contrast, contemporary concealed systems offer alternative approaches to spatial organization by integrating structural supports, cisterns, and plumbing connections within walls.

    The evolution of bathroom technology has transformed the relationship between sanitary fixtures, building infrastructure, and architectural surfaces. Traditional floor-mounted toilets and exposed plumbing systems have historically shaped bathroom configurations, with layouts largely determined by the placement of pipes and drainage connections. In contrast, contemporary concealed systems offer alternative approaches to spatial organization by integrating structural supports, cisterns, and plumbing connections within walls.

    This transition has implications beyond appearance. By separating visible fixtures from their supporting infrastructure, architects can develop more flexible layouts, simplify floor cleaning, and establish greater visual continuity between surfaces. Wall-hung toilets, for example, create an uninterrupted floor plane while allowing their installation height to be determined during construction. Nevertheless, these arrangements depend on the structural reliability, accessibility, and compatibility of components that remain largely invisible once installation is complete.

    Industry observers note that the evolution of bathroom technology reflects a shift in architectural priorities. Innovation is no longer expressed solely through visible fixtures, refined finishes, or increasingly automated equipment, but also through the development of reliable systems that enhance spatial flexibility, simplify installation, facilitate maintenance, and improve resource efficiency. Just as Kira questioned the relationship between standardized fixtures and the human body, contemporary innovations extend this discussion to the infrastructure that supports everyday activities. The challenge, therefore, lies in thoughtfully integrating technology into spaces that balance functionality, comfort, adaptability, and long-term performance.

    #229045. How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

    📅 22 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1487 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

    How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

    📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, you’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting.
    • It has been revealed that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships.
    • Sources indicate that going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, you’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting. For a while, that little phrase has been used to describe the experience of executing the bare minimum at work without actually leaving your job: You do just enough to get by but never rise above that benchmark to prove yourself or exceed expectations. It’s a strategy that can keep you employed while preserving your mental and emotional energy.

    It has been revealed that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships. And, yes, it could also apply to the one you have with your mom. Though you’re probably not collecting paychecks here, maintaining a relationship with your mother may connect you to important resources you need to get by. Maybe your mom really does play a substantial role in your finances, or she’s your source of health insurance. She could also be a connection to your culture or other family members that you don’t want to distance yourself from. Logistics aside, you might just want some distance from your mom without sacrificing your emotional connection. As I learned from reporting my book Motherf*cked: How to Keep Your Mother’s Toxic Drama From Ruining Your Life, those are all solid reasons to maintain a relationship that leaves you exhausted.

    Sources indicate that going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact. However, there’s no official definition, therapist Whitney Goodman, LMFT, told me in an interview for Motherf*cked. For some, it could look like avoiding one-on-one visits but checking in via text, email, quarterly phone calls, or greeting cards. Or you could catch up in person while avoiding the details of your life. The frequency of low-contact contact varies too. Some would say talking once a week is low-contact for them. Others might say once a year.

    The reasons why people go low-contact differ as much as the ways it can look. Generally speaking, taking space can be useful anytime a relationship feels painful or draining. It gives you more time, energy, and emotional bandwidth to take care of yourself and tend to other important parts of your life.

    Sources indicate that that can be especially helpful in our relationships with our moms, a dynamic that, for many reasons, is often packed with emotional triggers. If spending time with your mom feels exhausting, you’re sick of always stressing about this relationship, or you’ve tried and failed to set boundaries with her in the past, pulling back might be helpful here, Goodman states. If you can relate, here’s how to do that.

    Recent findings suggest that ideally, this process is a series of experiments where you pull back from the relationship in different ways to see what feels good and what doesn’t, Goodman explains. You can then use that information to determine how much contact is too much—or not enough. Here’s how to get started.

    Going low-contact is really just setting a boundary, or defining what behavior you will or won’t tolerate. You’re showing others how you want to be treated. Sometimes, people don’t like being restricted and get messy when limits are put on their relationships. Moms can be like that too.

    If you’ve already tried to set boundaries with your mom by, say, not answering every one of her calls or telling her that you don’t want to talk about your dating life, now is a good time to reflect on how that went.

    Industry observers note that moms who are receptive to those guardrails may be easygoing about any additional boundaries. That could mean you don’t need to cut as many points of contact to feel better about the relationship. On the other hand, if your mom has blown through your boundaries in the past, you might need stronger limitations to protect your peace today. Keep that in mind for the next step.

    Sources indicate that again, there is no official criterion defining a low-contact relationship, so don’t get hung up on labels. First, think about how much contact you have now. How often do you spend time together? What does that time look like? What would you change to make this relationship less taxing?

    Industry observers note that maybe you see your mom every Sunday, let her come over unannounced, and answer all of her texts—even the ones you’d rather not. Consider which of these interactions take the most out of you, and ask yourself, Would eliminating this point of contact make the relationship less exhausting overall?

    It has been revealed that you could start small by taking a beat to check in with yourself before responding to your mom’s texts. If you don’t feel like dealing with her at that moment, don’t. If that’s not enough to preserve your energy, maybe you can limit the number of texts you’ll respond to each day or week. You can always change it up later by removing another point of contact, like those unannounced visits, if you need more space (see step five).

    You don’t have to formally announce that you’re going low-contact, but giving your mom a heads-up might be useful.

    Sources indicate that if you’re not worried about your safety and your quiet quitting tactics mean your mom has to change her behavior, then laying out your intends could make sense. Plus, explaining why you put them in place might help you resolve whatever is behind your decision to quiet quit this relationship.

    That noted, if your version of low-contact doesn’t require anything from your mom, you don’t need to tell her it’s happening, states Goodman. For example, you can hold back information about your life or avoid certain events without discussing it first.

    Industry observers note that feel weird about this? I get that, but here’s something to think about: You’ve probably told your mom about the ways she’s hurt you many, many times before, claims Goodman. Even if you haven’t explicitly pointed to every single occasion she hurt your feelings, your body language and tone of voice likely have conveyed how her actions impacted you. You may be tired of retelling those painful events, which is why you’d like to avoid another confrontation with your mom. So consider this your permission not to.

    Still, your mom might notice you pulling back and ask what’s going on. If she does, you can tell her why you’re not getting into your dating life or attending the family reunion. You don’t have to, though. You’re welcome to make excuses or just say, “Yep, you’re right, I’m not doing that anymore.” You don’t owe her an explanation.

    Sources indicate that goodman says the best way to tell how going low-contact is working for you is to check in with your emotions as much as possible. You can write them down in your journal, use a mood- or emotions-tracking app, or bring them up to your therapist.

    In a recent development, yes, the feelings you’re tracking can be related to your mom and quiet quitting her, but don’t forget about all the others, says Goodman. It might not be obvious which feelings are related to your maternal figure and which aren’t. After breaking patterns that existed for a long time, you might get a sense that something is off. Maybe you feel purposeless or lost. Maybe it’s like you forgot something on your way to the airport, but you don’t know what it is.

    In a recent development, all of that is normal, indicates Goodman. So is feeling like you really miss your mom, even if you know you did the right thing. Of course, everyone’s situation is different. Maybe you don’t truly miss her, but miss the idea of a person she’ll never be. When quiet quitting is working, those feelings should come up less frequently and/or become less intense. At the same time, you’ll likely feel some relief. You could notice more peace in your life and more space to focus on things other than your mom.

    Industry observers note that you can always tweak how much contact you have with your mom. Ideally, this involves a continuous assessment of what’s working and what’s not. If the low-contact plan you’ve established feels sustainable and makes you less obsessive or overwhelmed by the relationship—and your mom is able to abide by your rules—you might have found a solution. Success!

    If this version of quiet quitting doesn’t keep your mom from violating your boundaries, emotionally manipulating you, or still leaves you drained, anxious, or depressed, you could level up, claims Goodman. That means starting back at step one and quitting other parts of your relationship until you reach a point that feels sustainable.

    Remember, the goal is for you to feel less stressed about your interactions with your mom. By finding a routine that works for you, you can protect the parts of your relationship that you love and lose the rest.

    Ambidestro clads coastal home in Brazil with rough local stone

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Contrasting volumes of smooth plaster and rough local Morelo stone define this coastal home in Brazil, designed by local architecture practice Ambidestro.
    • Named Casa Los Cobos, the home is located in Xangri-Lá on Brazil’s southern coast, and was designed to make the most of panoramic views out over the sea from the rear of the site.
    • Set back from the road, a series of routes both through and around the home “reveal the landscape gradually,” including a path beneath a timber canopy and via a paved veranda screened by lush plants.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Photography by Gabriel Konrath.

    Contrasting volumes of smooth plaster and rough local Morelo stone define this coastal home in Brazil, designed by local architecture practice Ambidestro.

    Named Casa Los Cobos, the home is located in Xangri-Lá on Brazil’s southern coast, and was designed to make the most of panoramic views out over the sea from the rear of the site.

    Set back from the road, a series of routes both through and around the home “reveal the landscape gradually,” including a path beneath a timber canopy and via a paved veranda screened by lush plants.

    “The main opportunity was the merging of two adjoining lots into a single site that extends to the rear, where the landscape opens onto the water,” Ambidestro co-founder João Pedro Crescente told Dezeen.

    The ground floor of Casa Los Cobos has been given over almost entirely to a single large living, dining and kitchen space, wrapped by service spaces and bathrooms.

    Full-height sliding glass doors allow this space to be opened out onto a large sheltered terrace alongside a swimming pool, with a lawn that slopes down to a nearby waterway.

    “The ground floor is free of partitions: living, dining and the entertaining kitchen are integrated and turned toward the greenery, accommodating everything from a weeknight dinner to a Saturday party,” Crescente told Dezeen.

    Industry observers note that “Between the living room and the water lie, in sequence, the veranda, the garden and the pool, which wraps around the house. The eye passes through these layers before reaching the backdrop,” he added.

    Both the exterior and interior have been given contrasting finishes of rough Morelo stone and white plaster and paint, with the rear terrace framed by white-painted masonry.

    This is complemented internally with bespoke carpentry in pale oak, including a floating timber bar supported by a concrete column that defines one edge of the living space.

    “The intention was to use natural, local materials in light, warm tones repeated inside and out, making the transition between spaces almost imperceptible,” remarked Crescente.

    “Moledo stone clads the facades and changes in appearance from morning to late afternoon. Other natural stones continue onto the floors and wet areas,” he added.

    A skylit staircase leads up to the more compartmentalised first floor of the home, which contains six en-suite bedrooms, two of which open onto a balcony overlooking the sea.

    To provide both shading and privacy from the road, sliding timber shutters can be pulled down over the full-height bedroom windows.

    Other homes in Brazil recently featured on Dezeen include a home in São Paolo by Studio Arthur Casas featuring dramatic overhangs and cantilevers, and a low-lying dwelling by Sabella Arquitetura that is topped by a gridded timber roof.

    Photography by Gabriel Konrath.

    📅 22 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1780 w)
